sections.heading: Laws of Chemical Combination, Mole Concept & Concentration Interconversions
sections.summary: One mole contains exactly N_A = 6.02214076 x 10^23 elementary entities and bridges mass, particle count, and ideal gas volume (22.4 L at old STP 1 atm/273.15 K; 22.7 L at IUPAC STP 1 bar/273.15 K). Temperature-independent concentration scales rely purely on masses, whereas volume-based scales vary with thermal expansion.
keyPoints: Laws: Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier), Definite Proportions (Proust), Multiple Proportions (Dalton: CO vs CO2), Reciprocal Proportions (Richter), Gay-Lussac Gaseous Volumes, Avogadro Hypothesis.

Temperature-independent scales: Molality m = (moles solute) / (kg solvent), Mole fraction X_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B), % w/w, and ppm by mass. Temperature-dependent scales: Molarity M, Normality N, % w/v, % v/v.
Exact M-to-m bridge: m = (1000 M) / (1000 d - M * M_solute), where d is solution density in g/mL and M_solute is molar mass in g/mol; for dilute aqueous solutions (d ~= 1), M ~= m.
Molarity of mixing: M_mix = (M1 V1 + M2 V2) / (V1 + V2) for non-reacting solutes; for acid-base mixing, compute net |mEq_acid - mEq_base| / V_total.
Combustion analysis for C_x H_y O_z: mass of C = (12/44) * m_CO2; mass of H = (2/18) * m_H2O; remaining mass = O. Divide % by atomic mass to get empirical formula.
Average atomic/molar mass: M_avg = sum(X_i M_i) = sum(%_i M_i) / 100; e.g. dry air (~78% N2, 21% O2, 1% Ar) has M_avg ~= 28.96 g/mol.

sections.heading: Stoichiometry, Limiting Reagent, POAC, Oleum & Eudiometry
sections.summary: Stoichiometric calculations require identifying the Limiting Reagent (LR) with the minimum (moles / stoichiometric coefficient) ratio before computing product yield. Principle of Atom Conservation (POAC) bypasses balancing complex multi-step cascades by conserving atoms of an element across reactants and products.
keyPoints: Limiting Reagent check: compare n_i / nu_i for all reactants; % Yield = (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) x 100; % Purity = (Pure mass / Impure sample mass) x 100.
POAC example: KClO3 -> KCl + O2 (unbalanced) satisfies 1 x n(KClO3) = 1 x n(KCl) and 3 x n(KClO3) = 2 x n(O2) directly.
Oleum (H2S2O7 = H2SO4 + SO3) labelling 'x%': 100 g oleum reacts with (x - 100) g H2O to give x g pure H2SO4. Free SO3 % = (80 / 18) * (x - 100); maximum label is 122.5% (100% SO3).
Volume strength of H2O2 (V): 1 L H2O2 gives V L O2 at NTP (22.4 L). Molarity M = V / 11.2, Normality N = V / 5.6, and % w/v = (34 * V) / 112 = 0.3036 V.
Hardness of water in ppm CaCO3 = [mass of CaCO3 eq (g) / mass of water (g)] x 10^6. Equivalent weights: Mg(HCO3)2 = 73, Ca(HCO3)2 = 81, CaSO4 = 68, MgCl2 = 47.5, CaCO3 = 50.

Eudiometry (gas explosion at constant T, P): Hydrocarbon C_x H_y + (x + y/4) O2 -> x CO2(g) + (y/2) H2O(l). Contraction on cooling = 1 + y/4 per mole; subsequent KOH/NaOH absorption equals x moles CO2; alkaline pyrogallol absorbs leftover O2.

sections.heading: Redox Reactions, Oxidation State Anomalies & Equivalent Concept
sections.summary: Oxidation involves electron loss (oxidation number increase) and reduction involves electron gain; in all balanced redox reactions, total equivalents of oxidant equal total equivalents of reductant (N1 V1 = N2 V2). Structural peroxide linkages and fractional average oxidation states explain apparent valence anomalies.
keyPoints: Oxidation state exceptions: CrO5 (butterfly structure, 2 peroxo -O-O- linkages -> Cr is +6, NOT +10); H2SO5 Caro's acid & H2S2O8 Marshall's acid (S is +6 with 1 peroxo bond); Na2S4O6 (terminal S = +5, central S = 0, avg = +2.5); Fe3O4 (FeO.Fe2O3: one Fe^2+ and two Fe^3+, avg = +8/3); CaOCl2 bleaching powder (Cl is +1 in OCl^- and -1 in Cl^-).

Disproportionation requires an intermediate oxidation state: P4 + 3 OH^- + 3 H2O -> PH3(-3) + 3 H2PO2^-(+1); Cl2 + 2 OH^-(cold dil) -> Cl^- + OCl^- + H2O; 3 Cl2 + 6 OH^-(hot conc) -> 5 Cl^- + ClO3^- + 3 H2O; F2 NEVER disproportionates (only -1).

n-factor of KMnO4: 5 in strong acid (MnO4^- -> Mn^2+, colourless), 3 in neutral/faintly alkaline (MnO4^- -> MnO2, brown ppt), 1 in strongly alkaline (MnO4^- -> MnO4^2-, dark green). K2Cr2O7 in acid: n = 6 (Cr2O7^2- orange -> 2 Cr^3+ green).
Dual oxidation n-factors: FeC2O4 -> Fe^3+ + 2 CO2 has n = 1 + 2 = 3; Cu2S -> 2 Cu^2+ + SO2 has n = 2(1) + 6 = 8; As2S3 -> 2 H3AsO4 + 3 SO4^2- has n = 2(2) + 3(8) = 28.

Iodimetry (direct I2 titration vs S2O3^2-) vs Iodometry (liberated I2 from excess KI by Cu^2+/MnO4^-/Cr2O7^2-/OCl^- titrated with Na2S2O3): 2 S2O3^2- + I2 -> S4O6^2- + 2 I^- (n-factor of Na2S2O3 = 1; starch indicator turns blue -> colourless at endpoint).
Back titration: excess reagent mEq added minus unreacted reagent mEq found by secondary titrant gives mEq of target analyte.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic Radiation, Photoelectric Effect & Bohr's Atomic Model
sections.summary: Planck's quantization (E = h*nu = hc/lambda) explains both the photoelectric threshold and discrete atomic emission spectra in one-electron species (H, He^+, Li^2+, Be^3+). Bohr's angular momentum quantization mvr = nh/(2pi) fixes circular radii, speeds, and negative bound-state energies.
keyPoints: Photoelectric Effect: h*nu = phi_0 + KE_max = h*nu_0 + e*V_s. Kinetic energy depends ONLY on frequency (> nu_0) and NOT on intensity; photocurrent is directly proportional to intensity (above nu_0).
Bohr formulas (Z = atomic number, n = orbit): r_n = 0.529 (n^2 / Z) A; v_n = 2.18 x 10^6 (Z / n) m/s; Time period T_n proportional to n^3 / Z^2; Frequency proportional to Z^2 / n^3.
Energy relations: E_n = -13.6 (Z^2 / n^2) eV/atom = -1312 (Z^2 / n^2) kJ/mol. Virial identity: Total Energy E = -KE = PE / 2 (so KE = |E|, PE = 2E).

Rydberg wavenumber: 1/lambda = R_H * Z^2 * (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) where R_H = 1.09677 x 10^7 m^(-1) (1/R_H ~= 911.6 A). Energy gap between n=1 and n=2 is 10.2 Z^2 eV; ionization energy from ground state = 13.6 Z^2 eV.

Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman (n1=1, UV), Balmer (n1=2, Visible), Paschen (n1=3, near-IR), Brackett (n1=4, IR), Pfund (n1=5, far-IR), Humphreys (n1=6, far-IR). First line (alpha) = longest lambda (n2 = n1+1); Series limit = shortest lambda (n2 = infinity).

Maximum spectral emission lines: from n2 to n1 = 1 gives n2(n2 - 1)/2 lines; between arbitrary n2 and n1 gives (n2 - n1)(n2 - n1 + 1)/2 lines. For a SINGLE atom dropping from n to 1, maximum emitted photons = n - 1.

sections.heading: Dual Nature, Heisenberg Uncertainty & Quantum Numbers
sections.summary: de Broglie matter waves (lambda = h/p) convert Bohr's orbit quantization into standing waves (2*pi*r_n = n*lambda), while Heisenberg's uncertainty principle prohibits exact simultaneous position and momentum measurements. Four quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, s) uniquely specify every electron's state.
keyPoints: de Broglie wavelength: lambda = h/(mv) = h/sqrt(2 m KE) = h/sqrt(2 m q V). For an electron accelerated through V volts: lambda ~= 12.27 / sqrt(V) A. Thermal neutron lambda = h / sqrt(3 m k_B T).
Heisenberg Uncertainty: dx * dp >= h/(4 pi) or dx * dv >= h/(4 pi m). Proves electron cannot reside inside nucleus (radius ~10^(-15) m requires velocity >> c).

Quantum Numbers: Principal n = 1,2,3... (shell size & H-atom energy); Azimuthal l = 0..n-1 (s=0, p=1, d=2, f=3; orbital angular momentum L = sqrt(l(l+1)) * h/(2pi)); Magnetic m_l = -l..+l (2l+1 orbitals, spatial orientation); Spin s = +1/2 or -1/2 (spin angular momentum S = sqrt(s(s+1)) * h/(2pi)).
Multi-electron energy follows (n + l) Bohr-Bury rule: lower (n+l) fills first; on tie, lower n fills first (e.g. 4s [4+0=4] fills before 3d [3+2=5], yet 4s electrons are ionized FIRST!).
Exchange energy & symmetry stabilize half-filled/full-filled configurations: Cr(24) = [Ar] 3d^5 4s^1; Cu(29) = [Ar] 3d^10 4s^1; Mo(42) = [Kr] 4d^5 5s^1; Pd(46) = [Kr] 4d^10 5s^0 (0 in 5s!).
Magnetic moment (spin-only): mu = sqrt(n_u (n_u + 2)) BM, where n_u is unpaired electrons (Fe^2+ d^6 -> n_u=4 -> 4.90 BM; Fe^3+/Mn^2+ d^5 -> n_u=5 -> 5.92 BM).

sections.heading: Schrodinger Wave Equation, Radial Wavefunctions & Nodal Surfaces
sections.summary: Solving H*Psi = E*Psi separates wavefunction Psi(r, theta, phi) = R_nl(r) * Y_lm(theta, phi), where Psi^2 represents electron probability density at a point and 4*pi*r^2*R^2 gives radial probability in a spherical shell. Nodes occur wherever R_nl(r) = 0 (radial spheres) or Y_lm = 0 (angular planes or cones).
keyPoints: Schrodinger equation in Cartesian: d^2Psi/dx^2 + d^2Psi/dy^2 + d^2Psi/dz^2 + (8 pi^2 m / h^2)(E - V) Psi = 0. Boundary condition: Psi is single-valued, continuous, finite, and zero at infinity.
Node counts: Radial (spherical) nodes = n - l - 1; Angular (non-spherical) nodes = l; Total nodes = n - 1. E.g. 4p has 2 radial + 1 angular = 3 total nodes; 3d has 0 radial + 2 angular = 2 nodes.

Angular nodal geometry: p_x (yz plane), p_y (xz plane), p_z (xy plane); d_xy (xz & yz), d_yz (xy & xz), d_xz (xy & yz), d_{x^2-y^2} (two planes at x = +/- y); d_{z^2} has TWO CONICAL nodal surfaces (3 cos^2(theta) - 1 = 0, theta = 54.7 deg), zero planar nodes!

1s radial wavefunction: R_1s(r) = 2 (Z/a_0)^(3/2) * e^(-Z r / a_0) -> Psi^2 is MAXIMUM at nucleus (r = 0), whereas radial probability 4*pi*r^2*Psi^2 is ZERO at r = 0 and peaks at r = a_0 / Z (0.529 A for H)!
2s radial wavefunction: R_2s proportional to (2 - Z r / a_0) * e^(-Z r / 2 a_0) -> vanishes at radial node r = 2 a_0 / Z. Number of peaks in 4*pi*r^2*R^2 vs r plot equals (n - l)!
Slater's Effective Nuclear Charge Z_eff = Z - sigma: penetration order s > p > d > f causes s-electrons to screen better and feel higher Z_eff at identical n.

solvedExamples.question: Calculate the molarity and molality of a 20% (w/w) aqueous NaOH solution having density 1.2 g/mL (NaOH = 40 g/mol).
steps: Assume 100 g of solution: mass of NaOH = 20 g (moles = 20 / 40 = 0.5 mol), mass of water = 80 g = 0.080 kg.
Volume of solution = mass / density = 100 g / (1.2 g/mL) = 83.33 mL = 0.08333 L.
Molality m = 0.5 mol / 0.080 kg = 6.25 m.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Dividing moles of solute by solution mass (0.1 kg) instead of solvent mass (0.08 kg) yields wrong molality 5.0 m.

solvedExamples.question: A mixture of 10 mL CH4 and 10 mL C2H4 is exploded with 60 mL O2 and cooled to room temperature. Find total volume of gas remaining and contraction after passing through aqueous KOH.
steps: CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O(l): 10 mL CH4 consumes 20 mL O2 and produces 10 mL CO2.
C2H4 + 3 O2 -> 2 CO2 + 2 H2O(l): 10 mL C2H4 consumes 30 mL O2 and produces 20 mL CO2.
Total O2 consumed = 20 + 30 = 50 mL => Leftover unreacted O2 = 60 - 50 = 10 mL.
Total CO2 formed = 10 + 20 = 30 mL; H2O condenses to liquid (~0 mL). Total gas after cooling = 30 + 10 = 40 mL; KOH absorbs all 30 mL CO2 leaving 10 mL O2.
solvedExamples.answer: 40 mL after cooling; 30 mL contraction in KOH (10 mL O2 left)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Treating H2O as gas below 100 deg C gives wrong post-cooling volume!

solvedExamples.question: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, s) is NOT permissible, and how many radial and angular nodes does the 4d_{x^2-y^2} orbital have? Sets: (A) (3, 2, -2, +1/2), (B) (4, 0, 0, -1/2), (C) (3, 3, -1, +1/2), (D) (2, 1, 0, +1/2).
steps: Check constraint l <= n - 1: in Set (C), n = 3 and l = 3 violates l <= 2 (no 3f subshell exists!).
Sets (A) 3d, (B) 4s, and (D) 2p satisfy n >= 1, 0 <= l <= n-1, |m_l| <= l, s = +/- 1/2.
Radial nodes = n - l - 1 = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1; Angular nodes = l = 2 planar nodes.
solvedExamples.answer: Set (C) is invalid; 4d_{x^2-y^2} has 1 radial node and 2 angular nodes
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing angular nodes (l) with total nodes (n - 1) leads to answering 3 angular nodes.

solvedExamples.question: Find the radial node distances (in terms of Bohr radius a_0) for a 3s orbital of a He^+ ion, whose radial wavefunction R_3s(r) is proportional to (27 - 18*sigma + 2*sigma^2)*e^(-sigma/3), where sigma = Z * r / a_0.
steps: At any radial node of 3s, R_3s(r) = 0, so 2*sigma^2 - 18*sigma + 27 = 0.
Since sigma = Z * r / a_0 and Z = 2 for He^+, the two spherical node radii are r_1 = 0.951 a_0 and r_2 = 3.549 a_0.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting to divide sigma by Z = 2 for He^+ gives double the true nodal radii.

sections.heading: Modern Periodic Table & Atomic/Ionic Radius Anomalies
sections.summary: Atomic radii decrease across a period due to rising effective nuclear charge Z_eff and increase down a group due to added principal shells, except where poor d/f shielding causes contractions. Ionic radii of isoelectronic species shrink monotonically as nuclear charge Z rises.
keyPoints: Radius definitions: Covalent radius < Metallic radius << van der Waals radius (Ne > F in Period 2 because noble gases use van der Waals radius!).
d-block contraction (Scandide contraction): Ga (135 pm) < Al (143 pm) because intervening 3d^10 electrons shield nuclear charge poorly.
Lanthanoid contraction (poor 4f shielding): 4d and 5d pairs have nearly identical radii -> Zr ~= Hf, Nb ~= Ta, Mo ~= W (causes 5d metals to have very high density).
Isoelectronic series (10 e-): Al^3+ < Mg^2+ < Na^+ < F^- < O^2- < N^3- (higher Z/e ratio pulls electron cloud tighter).
Transition period 3d radii: Sc > Ti > V > Cr > Mn ~= Fe ~= Co ~= Ni < Cu < Zn (inter-electronic d-d repulsion causes slight expansion at Cu, Zn).
IUPAC >100 naming roots: 0=nil, 1=un, 2=bi, 3=tri, 4=quad, 5=pent, 6=hex, 7=sept, 8=oct, 9=enn; e.g., Z=119 Ununennium (Uue).

sections.heading: Ionization Enthalpy, Electron Gain Enthalpy & Oxide Character
sections.summary: Half-filled and completely-filled subshells create sharp discontinuities in Period 2 and 3 ionization enthalpies, while compact 2p electron-electron repulsion makes Period 3 halogens/chalcogens release more energy on electron gain than Period 2.
keyPoints: IE1 Period 2: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne (Be > B due to penetrating 2s^2; N > O due to half-filled 2p^3). Period 3: Na < Al < Mg < Si < S < P < Cl < Ar.
Group 13 IE1 anomaly: B > Tl > Ga > Al > In (d-contraction raises Ga above Al; 4f lanthanoid contraction raises Tl above Ga, Al, In!). Group 14 IE1: C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn (Pb > Sn!).
Successive IE jump reveals valence electron count: e.g. massive jump between IE2 and IE3 identifies Group 2 (ns^2). Note IE2 order: O^+ > N^+ (because O^+ is half-filled 2p^3!).

Electron Gain Enthalpy (magnitude of exothermic Delta_eg H): Halogens Cl > F > Br > I; Chalcogens S > Se > Te > Po > O (O has LEAST negative EGE in Group 16!); Group 15 N has ~0/positive EGE; Noble gases have positive Delta_eg H (Ne highest!).

Electronegativity: Pauling scale F(4.0) > O(3.5) > N ~= Cl(3.0) > Br(2.8) > C ~= S ~= I(2.5) > H(2.1). Mulliken EN = (IE + EA) / 2 in eV; Pauling EN ~= Mulliken / 2.8. Carbon EN rises with %s: sp (3.25) > sp2 (2.75) > sp3 (2.5).
Oxide nature: Basic (Na2O, CaO, MgO, MnO); Acidic (CO2, SO3, Cl2O7, Mn2O7, CrO3); Amphoteric (BeO, Al2O3, Ga2O3, ZnO, SnO, SnO2, PbO, PbO2, Cr2O3, V2O5, As2O3); Neutral (CO, NO, N2O).

sections.heading: Ionic Bonding, Lattice Enthalpy, Hydration & Fajan's Polarization
sections.summary: Ionic solids stabilize via Madelung lattice enthalpy U proportional to (q+ * q-) / (r+ + r-), while covalent character creeps into ionic bonds whenever small, highly charged cations distort large polarizable anions (Fajan's rules).
keyPoints: Born-Haber Cycle: Delta_f H = Delta_sub H + IE + (1/2)BDE + Delta_eg H + U_lattice (where U is negative formation enthalpy). Lattice energy: MgO > NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI.

Solubility rule: Compound dissolves when |Delta_hyd H| > |U_lattice|. Small-small or large-large mismatch: BeSO4 > MgSO4 > CaSO4 > SrSO4 > BaSO4 (hydration dominates), whereas Be(OH)2 < Mg(OH)2 < Ca(OH)2 < Ba(OH)2 (lattice dominates).

Fajan's Polarization Rules (higher covalent character -> lower MP, lower water solubility, deeper colour): Small cation (LiCl > NaCl), Large anion (LiI > LiBr > LiCl > LiF), High charge (AlCl3 > MgCl2 > NaCl), Pseudo-noble gas d^10 shell (CuCl, AgCl, HgCl2 >> NaCl, KCl).
Colour via polarization: AgF (white, ionic) -> AgCl (white) -> AgBr (pale yellow) -> AgI (bright yellow); similarly SnI4 (orange-red), PbI2 (golden yellow), HgI2 (scarlet red).

Thermal stability of oxy-salts (CO3^2-, NO3^-, OH^-, SO4^2-): Increases DOWN the group as cation size grows and polarizing power falls (Li2CO3 decomposes easily to Li2O + CO2; Na2CO3 is thermally stable; BeCO3 kept in CO2 atmosphere).

sections.heading: VSEPR Shapes, Hybridization, Bent's Rule & Drago's Rule
sections.summary: Steric number SN = sigma bonds + lone pairs (or 1/2[V + M - C + A]) fixes electron-pair geometry, while lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp repulsion and Bent's rule dictate exact bond angles and axial/equatorial preferences.
keyPoints: Key VSEPR geometries: SN=4 (CH4 tetrahedral 109.5, NH3 pyramidal 107, H2O bent 104.5); SN=5 (PCl5 TBP, SF4 see-saw, ClF3 T-shaped, XeF2 / I3^- / ICl2^- linear); SN=6 (SF6 octahedral, BrF5 / XeOF4 sq pyramidal, XeF4 / ICl4^- sq planar); SN=7 (IF7 PBP, XeF6 capped/distorted octahedral with 1 lp).

Bent's Rule: More electronegative substituents (F, Cl, OH) prefer hybrid orbitals with LOWER s-character (hence occupy AXIAL positions in sp3d TBP: PCl3F2 puts both F axial -> dipole = 0!); lone pairs and double bonds demand HIGHER s-character (equatorial in TBP).

Bond angle trends: CH4(109.5) > NH3(107) > H2O(104.5); NO2^+(180) > NO2(134) > NO2^-(115); NH3(107) > NF3(102.5) due to electronegativity pulling bp away; PF3 < PCl3 < PBr3 < PI3 (lp repulsion + steric); OCl2(110.9) > H2O(104.5) due to steric crowding / Cl back-bonding.

Drago's Rule: Period 3+ central atoms bonded to less electronegative H (EN <= 2.5) undergo NO hybridization -> pure p-orbitals give ~90 deg angles: PH3(93.6), AsH3(91.8), SbH3(91.3), H2S(92.1), H2Se(91).

Odd-electron molecules: NO2 (sp2, 134 deg, unpaired e- in sp2 orbital -> dimerizes to N2O4); ClO2 (unpaired e- delocalized in d-pi orbital -> does NOT dimerize); CF3 radical (sp3 pyramidal) vs CH3 radical (sp2 planar).
Solid-state ionic dimers: PCl5(s) exists as [PCl4]^+(Td) [PCl6]^-(Oh); PBr5(s) = [PBr4]^+ Br^-; N2O5(s) = [NO2]^+(linear) [NO3]^-(planar); I2Cl6(s) = planar bridged dimer.

sections.heading: Dipole Moment, Resonance, Back Bonding & Banana Bonding
sections.summary: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles and lone-pair moments, so symmetric geometries cancel individual polar bonds to zero. Unfilled vacant p/d orbitals on adjacent atoms enable ppi-ppi or ppi-dpi back bonding that flattens geometries and tunes Lewis acidity.
keyPoints: Zero dipole moment despite polar bonds: CO2, CS2, BeCl2, BF3, SO3, CH4, CCl4, SF6, PF5, PCl3F2, XeF2, XeF4, trans-1,2-dichloroethene, p-dichlorobenzene (o > m > p = 0).
NH3 (1.47 D) >> NF3 (0.23 D): in NH3, N-H bond dipoles reinforce the N lone-pair dipole; in NF3, three N-F bond dipoles oppose the lone-pair dipole!
Boron trihalide Lewis acidity: BF3 < BCl3 < BBr3 < BI3 (REVERSE of electronegativity!). Strongest 2p-2p back-bonding in BF3 reduces boron's electron deficiency most effectively.

Geometry flattening via 2p-3d back-bonding: N(CH3)3 is pyramidal (sp3, 108 deg) and strongly basic, whereas N(SiH3)3 is PLANAR (sp2, 120 deg) and non-basic! Similarly (SiH3)2O has wide ~144 deg Si-O-Si angle vs H2O 104.5 deg.

Hydrolysis contrast: CCl4 does NOT hydrolyze (no vacant d-orbitals), whereas SiCl4/PCl3/SF4 hydrolyze vigorously; SF6 is kinetically inert to H2O due to steric shielding of 6 F atoms (unlike SeF6/TeF6).
Bridged dimers: B2H6 has two 3c-2e B-H-B banana bonds (electron-deficient); Al2Cl6 & BeCl2(g) dimer have 3c-4e coordinate Cl-bridges (electron-precise).

sections.heading: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT), Bond Order & Hydrogen Bonding
sections.summary: Linear combination of atomic orbitals produces bonding (sigma, pi) and antibonding (sigma*, pi*) MOs, directly predicting bond order, stability, and paramagnetism. Hydrogen bonds formed by H attached to F, O, or N drastically raise boiling points and alter volatility between isomers.
keyPoints: s-p mixing (<= 14 e-: Li2 to N2): sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < (pi2px = pi2py) < sigma2pz < (pi*2px = pi*2py) < sigma*2pz. Thus B2 (10 e-) has 2 unpaired electrons in pi2p (PARAMAGNETIC); C2 (12 e-) has BO = 2 made purely of TWO pi bonds (diamagnetic!).

Without s-p mixing (> 14 e-: O2, F2, Ne2): sigma2pz drops BELOW (pi2px = pi2py). O2 (16 e-) has 2 unpaired e- in pi*2p (paramagnetic, BO=2). O2^+ (BO=2.5, shorter) > O2 (2.0) > O2^- (1.5) > O2^2- (1.0, diamagnetic!).
Heteronuclear MOT: CO (14 e-, BO=3) -> CO^+ has BO = 3.5 (anomalous slightly higher than CO because HOMO has antibonding character!); NO (15 e-, BO=2.5, paramag) -> NO^+ (14 e-, BO=3, diamag).
He2 has BO = 0 (does not exist), while H2^+, He2^+, H2^- all have BO = 0.5; stability H2^+ > H2^- because H2^- has an antibonding electron!

Intermolecular H-bonding raises BP/MP/viscosity: H2O (100 deg C, 4 H-bonds/molecule in 3D cage -> ice floats!) > HF (19.5 deg C, zig-zag chains) > NH3 (-33 deg C); p-nitrophenol has high BP & water solubility.

Intramolecular H-bonding (chelation) lowers BP & boosts steam volatility: o-nitrophenol (steam-volatile, separates from p-nitrophenol!), o-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde), KHF2 ([F-H-F]^- strongest symmetric H-bond!), chloral hydrate CCl3CH(OH)2.

solvedExamples.question: Predict the hybridization, molecular shape, number of lone pairs on central atom, and polarity of XeOF4 and I3^-.
steps: For XeOF4: SN = (8 + 4 - 0 + 0)/2 = 6 (oxygen is divalent so M = 4 from F atoms only).
Surrounded atoms = 5 (1 O + 4 F) => Lone pairs = 6 - 5 = 1; Hybridization = sp3d2; Shape = Square Pyramidal (polar, non-zero dipole).
For I3^- (central I with two terminal I): SN = (7 + 2 + 1)/2 = 5 => sp3d.
Surrounded atoms = 2 => Lone pairs = 5 - 2 = 3 (all 3 occupy equatorial positions); Shape = Linear (180 deg, non-polar).
solvedExamples.answer: XeOF4: sp3d2, Square Pyramidal, 1 LP, Polar; I3^-: sp3d, Linear, 3 LP, Non-polar
solvedExamples.pitfall: Counting divalent Oxygen in M of SN = (V+M-C+A)/2 gives wrong SN = 7!

solvedExamples.question: Arrange the following in increasing order of O-O bond length and magnetic nature: KO2, BaO2, O2, O2[AsF6].
steps: Identify oxygen species: O2[AsF6] has O2^+; O2 is neutral; KO2 is superoxide O2^-; BaO2 is peroxide O2^2-.
Compute MOT bond orders: O2^+ = 2.5, O2 = 2.0, O2^- = 1.5, O2^2- = 1.0.
Higher bond order gives shorter bond length: O2^+ < O2 < O2^- < O2^2-.
Magnetic nature: O2^+ (1 unpaired pi*), O2 (2 unpaired pi*), O2^- (1 unpaired pi*) are paramagnetic; ONLY BaO2 (O2^2-, 0 unpaired) is diamagnetic.
solvedExamples.answer: O2[AsF6] < O2 < KO2 < BaO2 (only BaO2 is diamagnetic)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Thinking KO2 is peroxide (K is +1, so O2^- is superoxide!) flips both bond order and magnetism.

solvedExamples.question: Among BeCO3, MgCO3, CaCO3, and BaCO3, which has the highest thermal stability and why? Also identify which among Be(OH)2, Ba(OH)2, BeSO4, BaSO4 is most soluble in water.
steps: Polarizing power of cation (charge/size) decreases down Group 2: Be^2+ > Mg^2+ > Ca^2+ > Ba^2+.
Be^2+ strongly polarizes CO3^2- distortion toward O^2- + CO2, giving lowest decomposition temperature; BaCO3 has maximum thermal stability.
For hydroxides (small OH^-): lattice energy drops faster than hydration energy down the group -> Ba(OH)2 is most soluble.
For sulphates (large SO4^2-): lattice energy stays nearly constant while hydration enthalpy drops sharply -> BeSO4 is most soluble (BaSO4 insoluble!).
solvedExamples.answer: Thermal stability max: BaCO3; Most soluble hydroxide: Ba(OH)2; Most soluble sulphate: BeSO4
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying the same solubility direction to both hydroxides and sulphates in Group 2!

solvedExamples.question: Compare the axial vs equatorial P-X bond lengths in PCl3F2 and PCl2F3, and determine which molecule has zero dipole moment.
steps: Both molecules have SN = 5 (sp3d, Trigonal Bipyramidal geometry).
By Bent's rule, more electronegative F atoms prefer axial orbitals (pure p_z character, 0% s) while Cl prefers equatorial orbitals (~33% s).

In PCl3F2: BOTH F atoms sit axially (180 deg apart) and all 3 Cl atoms sit symmetrically at 120 deg in the equatorial plane => net dipole = 0! Axial P-F bonds are elongated relative to equatorial P-Cl.
In PCl2F3: two F sit axially and the 3rd F sits equatorially alongside two Cl atoms => equatorial F pulls dipole differently from two Cl => non-zero dipole moment! Also P-F(axial) > P-F(equatorial).
solvedExamples.answer: PCl3F2 has zero dipole moment; PCl2F3 is polar; in both, axial bonds are longer than equatorial bonds of the same element
solvedExamples.pitfall: Placing Cl axially in PCl3F2 violates Bent's rule and falsely predicts a polar molecule.

sections.heading: First Law of Thermodynamics, Expansion Work & Heat Capacities
sections.summary: The First Law (Delta U = q + w in IUPAC Chemistry sign convention, where w = -P_ext * dV) tracks internal energy conservation across reversible and irreversible paths. Work and heat are path functions, whereas U, H, S, and G are exact state functions.
keyPoints: IUPAC Chemistry Convention: heat absorbed q > 0, work done ON system w > 0, expansion work w < 0. (Never mix Physics dU = q - W with Chemistry dU = q + w!).

Isothermal Ideal Gas (Delta U = 0, Delta H = 0): w_rev = -n R T ln(V2/V1) = -2.303 n R T log10(P1/P2); w_irr = -P_ext (V2 - V1). Free expansion into vacuum (P_ext = 0) gives w = 0, q = 0, Delta U = 0.
Magnitude comparison: |w_rev| > |w_irr| during EXPANSION (more work extracted), whereas |w_rev| < |w_irr| during COMPRESSION (less work needed reversibly).

Adiabatic Process (q = 0, Delta U = w): Reversible satisfies P V^gamma = const, T V^(gamma-1) = const, and w_rev = n C_v (T2 - T1) = (P2 V2 - P1 V1) / (gamma - 1). Irreversible uses w_irr = -P_ext (V2 - V1) = n C_v (T2 - T1) directly!
Heat capacities: C_p - C_v = R (ideal gas); gamma = C_p / C_v (monatomic 5/3 = 1.67, diatomic 7/5 = 1.40, linear polyatomic 1.40 at RT, non-linear 4/3 = 1.33).
Kirchhoff's Equation: Delta H(T2) - Delta H(T1) = Delta C_p (T2 - T1), where Delta C_p = Sum C_p(products) - Sum C_p(reactants).

sections.heading: Thermochemistry, Hess's Law & Standard Enthalpy Variants
sections.summary: Enthalpy H = U + PV converts constant-volume bomb calorimeter data (q_v = Delta U) to constant-pressure reaction heats (q_p = Delta H = Delta U + Delta n_g RT). Hess's Law allows algebraic addition of thermochemical equations because enthalpy is a state function.
keyPoints: Delta n_g = (moles of GASEOUS products) - (moles of GASEOUS reactants); strictly ignore solids and liquids!

Standard Enthalpy of Formation (Delta_f H deg): 1 mole compound formed from stable reference elements at 298 K, 1 bar. Zero ONLY for O2(g), H2(g), C(graphite), S8(rhombic), P4(white), Br2(l), Hg(l), I2(s). Diamond != 0!
Standard Enthalpy of Combustion (Delta_c H deg): complete combustion of 1 mole substance in excess O2 (always exothermic, < 0). Higher calorific value / lower stability gives more negative Delta_c H.

Bond Enthalpy shortcut: Delta H_rxn = Sum BE(reactants) - Sum BE(products) (valid strictly for gas-phase molecules; subtract resonance energy if aromatic/conjugated: RE = |Delta H_exp - Delta H_calc|).

Enthalpy of Neutralization: Strong acid + Strong base = -57.3 kJ/mol (-13.7 kcal/mol) per mole H2O formed. Weak acid/base drops magnitude due to ionization heat, EXCEPT HF + NaOH = -68.6 kJ/mol (massive hydration of tiny F^-!).
Lattice & Solution bridge: Delta_sol H = Delta_lattice H + Delta_hyd H (Note: U_lattice defined positively when breaking crystal, negatively when forming).

sections.heading: Second & Third Laws, Entropy (Delta S) & Gibbs Spontaneity (Delta G)
sections.summary: A process is spontaneous only if total universe entropy increases (Delta S_total = Delta S_sys + Delta S_surr > 0), which translates at constant T and P into negative Gibbs free energy change (Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S < 0).
keyPoints: Entropy change (ideal gas reversible): Delta S = n C_v ln(T2/T1) + n R ln(V2/V1) = n C_p ln(T2/T1) - n R ln(P2/P1). For isothermal mixing of ideal gases: Delta S_mix = -R Sum(n_i ln X_i) > 0.
Phase transitions (reversible at equilibrium T_m or T_b): Delta S_fus = Delta H_fus / T_m; Delta S_vap = Delta H_vap / T_b (Trouton's rule: ~85-88 J/(mol.K) for non-H-bonded liquids).
Surroundings entropy: Delta S_surr = -Delta H_sys / T_surr. Even if Delta S_sys < 0 (e.g. freezing water below 0 C), exothermic heat raises Delta S_surr enough so Delta S_univ > 0.
Spontaneity signs (Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S): (-H, +S) always spontaneous; (+H, -S) never spontaneous; (-H, -S) spontaneous at LOW T (< dH/dS); (+H, +S) spontaneous at HIGH T (> dH/dS).
Equilibrium & Van't Hoff link: Delta G = Delta G deg + R T ln Q; at equilibrium Delta G = 0 => Delta G deg = -2.303 R T log10(K_eq). Also ln(K2/K1) = (-Delta H deg / R)(1/T2 - 1/T1).
Third Law of Thermodynamics: Entropy of a pure, perfectly crystalline substance approaches ZERO as T -> 0 K (CO, NO, N2O retain residual entropy due to orientation disorder).

sections.heading: Gas Solubility (Henry's Law), Raoult's Law & Azeotropes
sections.summary: Henry's law (p = K_H * X) governs gas dissolution in liquids, while Raoult's law relates partial vapour pressures of miscible liquid mixtures to mole fractions. Strong or weak A-B interactions induce negative or positive deviations, creating constant-boiling azeotropes.
keyPoints: Henry's Law: p = K_H * X_gas. Higher K_H means LOWER solubility! Raising temperature increases K_H, reducing gas solubility (aquatic species prefer cold water; scuba divers suffer 'bends' from N2 decompression; He dilutes tanks).

Raoult's Law (volatile liquids A + B): P_total = P_A deg X_A + P_B deg X_B = P_B deg + (P_A deg - P_B deg) X_A. Vapour-phase mole fraction Y_A = P_A / P_total (always richer in MORE volatile component!).
Ideal Solutions (Delta H_mix = 0, Delta V_mix = 0, Delta S_mix > 0, Delta G_mix < 0): n-hexane + n-heptane, bromoethane + chloroethane, benzene + toluene.

Positive Deviation (A-B weaker than A-A/B-B; P_obs > P_Raoult; Delta H_mix > 0, Delta V_mix > 0): Ethanol + H2O, Ethanol + Cyclohexane, Acetone + CS2, Acetone + Ethanol -> forms MINIMUM boiling azeotrope (e.g. 95.6% EtOH + 4.4% H2O boils at 78.15 C).

Negative Deviation (A-B H-bonding stronger; P_obs < P_Raoult; Delta H_mix < 0, Delta V_mix < 0): Chloroform + Acetone (C-H...O=C H-bond!), HNO3 + H2O (68% HNO3 max boiling 120.5 C), HCl + H2O, Phenol + Aniline.
Azeotrope behaviour: Boils at constant temperature with identical liquid and vapour compositions (X_A = Y_A); CANNOT be separated by fractional distillation!

sections.heading: Colligative Properties & Van't Hoff Factor (i)
sections.summary: Colligative properties depend strictly on the total number of solute particles per solvent quantity, requiring multiplication by the Van't Hoff factor i = M_normal / M_abnormal whenever electrolytes dissociate or solutes dimerize.
keyPoints: Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure (RLVP): (P deg - P_s)/P deg = i*n_solute / (i*n_solute + n_solvent); dilute form ~= i * X_solute. (P deg - P_s)/P_s = i*n_solute / n_solvent is EXACT!

Elevation of Boiling Point: Delta T_b = i * K_b * m; Depression of Freezing Point: Delta T_f = i * K_f * m. Thermodynamic constants: K_b = (R T_b^2 M_solvent) / (1000 * Delta_vap H); for water K_b = 0.52, K_f = 1.86 K.kg/mol.
Osmotic Pressure: pi = i * C * R * T = (i * n_2 / V) R T. Best method for molar mass of proteins/polymers because measurable pressure works at room temperature without thermal degradation.

Biological osmosis: Isotonic (equal pi, e.g. 0.9% w/v NaCl saline); Hypertonic (higher pi -> RBCs shrink/crenate); Hypotonic (lower pi -> RBCs swell/hemolyze). Reverse Osmosis occurs when P_applied > pi.

Van't Hoff Factor i: Dissociation into n ions -> i = 1 + (n - 1)alpha (100% NaCl i=2, BaCl2 i=3, K4[Fe(CN)6] i=5). Association of n molecules -> i = 1 + (1/n - 1)alpha (Benzoic acid/acetic acid in benzene dimerizes n=2 -> i = 1 - alpha/2).
Cryoscopic ranking at equal molality: Higher (i * m) gives LOWER vapour pressure, LOWER freezing point, HIGHER boiling point, and HIGHER osmotic pressure!

solvedExamples.question: For a reaction 2 A(g) + B(g) -> 2 D(g), Delta U deg = -10.5 kJ and Delta S deg = -44.1 J/K at 298 K. Calculate Delta G deg and state whether reaction is spontaneous at 298 K (R = 8.314 J/mol.K).

sections.heading: Chemical Equilibrium: Law of Mass Action, Kp/Kc & Vapour Density
sections.summary: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse rates become equal so macroscopic concentrations stay constant and reaction quotient Q equals K_eq. Equilibrium constant K depends EXCLUSIVELY on temperature and balanced stoichiometry.
keyPoints: Kp = Kc (R T)^(Delta n_g) and Kp = Kx * P^(Delta n_g), where Delta n_g excludes pure solids and liquids (activity = 1).
Stoichiometric manipulations: reversing reaction gives 1/K; multiplying by m raises K -> K^m; adding two steps multiplies K_net = K1 * K2.
Reaction Quotient Q vs K: Q < K shifts forward; Q = K equilibrium; Q > K shifts backward.

Degree of Dissociation (alpha) via Vapour Density: D_theoretical / d_observed = 1 + (n - 1)alpha, where n is gas moles formed from 1 mole reactant (for PCl5 -> PCl3 + Cl2, n = 2 => alpha = (D - d)/d).
Dissociation constants: PCl5 at total P gives Kp = (alpha^2 P)/(1 - alpha^2); N2O4 -> 2 NO2 gives Kp = (4 alpha^2 P)/(1 - alpha^2); 2 NH3 <-> N2 + 3H2 gives Kp proportional to alpha^4 P^2.
Simultaneous equilibria: e.g. NH4HS(s) <-> NH3 + H2S and NH2COONH4(s) <-> 2 NH3 + CO2 share common NH3 partial pressure so use total [NH3] in BOTH Kp expressions!

sections.heading: Le Chatelier's Principle & Thermodynamic Temperature Shifts
sections.summary: When a system at equilibrium suffers a stress in concentration, pressure, or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the imposed change. Catalysts accelerate both forward and reverse rates identically, shortening attainment time without shifting K.
keyPoints: Adding/removing species: adding reactant shifts forward; adding pure solid/liquid causes ZERO shift (active mass = 1).
Pressure / Volume change: increasing total P (decreasing V) shifts toward FEWER gaseous moles (Delta n_g < 0 favored); if Delta n_g = 0 (H2 + I2 <-> 2HI), pressure causes ZERO shift.

Inert gas addition trap: At CONSTANT VOLUME, partial pressures of all species stay unchanged -> ZERO shift! At CONSTANT PRESSURE, total volume expands so partial pressures drop -> shifts toward MORE gas moles!
Temperature effect (van't Hoff): Raising T ALWAYS favors the ENDOTHERMIC direction (Delta H > 0 -> K increases); lowering T favors EXOTHERMIC (Delta H < 0).
Industrial applications: Haber NH3 (N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, Delta H < 0 -> high P, optimal ~700 K, Fe/Mo catalyst); Contact SO3 (2SO2 + O2 <-> 2SO3, Delta H < 0 -> high P, ~720 K, V2O5).

sections.heading: Acids-Bases, Water Auto-Ionization & Exact pH Calculations
sections.summary: Bronsted-Lowry conjugate pairs satisfy K_a * K_b = K_w (pKa + pKb = pKw = 14 at 298 K), while Lewis acids accept lone pairs (BF3, AlCl3, Fe^3+) and Lewis bases donate them. Exact pH requires accounting for water auto-ionization in ultra-dilute (< 10^-6 M) solutions.
keyPoints: Water Kw = [H^+][OH^-] = 10^(-14) at 25 deg C (neutral pH = 7). Because H2O <-> H^+ + OH^- is endothermic, raising T increases Kw (at 90 deg C, Kw ~= 10^(-12) -> neutral water has pH = 6, still neutral because [H^+] = [OH^-]!).
Ostwald Dilution Law (weak acid HA): alpha = sqrt(K_a / C) when alpha <= 0.05; [H^+] = sqrt(K_a * C); exact quadratic [H^+]^2 + K_a[H^+] - K_a C = 0.
Ultra-dilute strong acid trap: 10^(-8) M HCl -> solve [H^+] = C_acid + Kw/[H^+] => [H^+] = 1.05 x 10^(-7) M => pH = 6.98 (< 7, NEVER 8!). Similarly 10^(-8) M NaOH gives pH = 7.02!
Mixture of two weak acids (HA1, HA2): [H^+] = sqrt(C1 Ka1 + C2 Ka2). Strong acid + Weak acid: common ion suppresses weak acid ionization.
Polyprotic acids (H3PO4: Ka1 >> Ka2 >> Ka3): first dissociation controls pH; [A^2-] at equilibrium ~= Ka2 (independent of dilution for H2CO3/H2S!).
Relative strengths: HClO4 > HI > HBr > HCl > H2SO4 > HNO3 (in water, leveling effect equalizes strong acids; in glacial CH3COOH, HClO4 > HBr > H2SO4 > HCl > HNO3).

sections.heading: Salt Hydrolysis, Buffers, Amphiprotic Salts & Titration Indicators
sections.summary: Conjugate ions of weak acids or bases hydrolyze water to shift pH away from 7, whereas buffer mixtures resist pH changes upon dilution or small acid/base additions via Henderson-Hasselbalch equilibrium.
keyPoints: 4 Salt Hydrolysis regimes: SA+SB (NaCl, pH = 7); WA+SB (CH3COONa: K_h = K_w/K_a, pH = 7 + 0.5(pKa + log C)); SA+WB (NH4Cl: K_h = K_w/K_b, pH = 7 - 0.5(pKb + log C)); WA+WB (CH3COONH4: K_h = K_w/(K_a*K_b), pH = 7 + 0.5(pKa - pKb), independent of C!).
Amphiprotic salts (NaHCO3, NaHS, NaH2PO4, Na2HPO4): pH = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2 (exact when C >> Ka1, independent of concentration).
Acidic Buffer (HA + NaA): pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]). Basic Buffer (BOH + BCl): pOH = pKb + log([Salt]/[Base]). Effective range: pKa +/- 1; Maximum buffer capacity at [Salt] = [Acid] (pH = pKa).
Diluting an ideal buffer moderately leaves [Salt]/[Acid] unchanged -> pH remains nearly constant!

Titration Equivalence Points & Indicators (range pK_In +/- 1): SA vs SB (pH jump 3.5-10.5 -> either Methyl Orange or Phenolphthalein works); WA vs SB (equivalence pH > 7 -> Phenolphthalein 8.3-10.0 ONLY!); WB vs SA (equivalence pH < 7 -> Methyl Orange 3.1-4.4 ONLY!).

sections.heading: Solubility Product (Ksp), Common Ion Effect & Selective Precipitation
sections.summary: A sparingly soluble salt M_x A_y precipitates only when its ionic product Q_sp = [M^(y+)]^x [A^(x-)]^y exceeds K_sp, while adding a common ion sharply lowers molar solubility S without changing K_sp.
keyPoints: K_sp vs Molar Solubility S: AB (AgCl, BaSO4) -> S^2; A2B/AB2 (PbI2, Ag2CrO4) -> 4 S^3; A3B/AB3 (Fe(OH)3, Al(OH)3) -> 27 S^4; A3B2 (Ca3(PO4)2) -> 108 S^5.
Precipitation conditions: Q_sp < K_sp (unsaturated, no ppt); Q_sp = K_sp (saturated); Q_sp > K_sp (precipitation until Q_sp = K_sp).
Common ion suppression: Solubility of AgCl in 0.1 M NaCl is S = K_sp / 0.1 (NOT sqrt(K_sp)!). Check both [Ag^+] and [Cl^-] contributions when C_common is tiny.

Selective sulphide precipitation: H2S in acidic medium (HCl, Group II) suppresses [S^2-] via [H^+]^2 * [S^2-] = K1*K2*[H2S] so only low-Ksp sulphides (CuS, PbS, CdS) precipitate; alkaline NH4OH (Group IV) raises [S^2-] to precipitate ZnS, MnS, NiS, CoS.
Hydrolysis & complexation raise solubility: AgCl dissolves in aq. NH3 via [Ag(NH3)2]^+ (K_net = K_sp * K_f); AgCN/CaF2/CH3COOAg dissolve better in strong acid because anion protonates!

solvedExamples.question: Calculate the pH of the resulting solution when 50 mL of 0.2 M CH3COOH (pKa = 4.74) is mixed with 50 mL of 0.2 M NaOH.
steps: Initial mmoles: CH3COOH = 50 x 0.2 = 10 mmol; NaOH = 50 x 0.2 = 10 mmol.
Exact neutralization occurs! Remaining acid = 0, remaining base = 0; formed CH3COONa = 10 mmol.
Total volume = 50 + 50 = 100 mL => [CH3COONa] C = 10 mmol / 100 mL = 0.1 M.
Apply WA+SB salt hydrolysis: pH = 7 + 0.5(pKa + log C) = 7 + 0.5(4.74 + log 0.1) = 7 + 0.5(3.74) = 8.87.

solvedExamples.question: An aqueous solution contains 0.01 M Cu^2+ and 0.01 M Zn^2+ saturated with H2S (0.1 M; K_a1 * K_a2 = 10^(-20)). K_sp(CuS) = 10^(-36) and K_sp(ZnS) = 10^(-22). Find the exact pH range in which ONLY CuS precipitates while Zn^2+ remains completely in solution.
steps: From H2S overall equilibrium: [H^+]^2 [S^2-] = K_a1 * K_a2 * [H2S] = 10^(-20) * 0.1 = 10^(-21).
Minimum [S^2-] to begin CuS precipitation: [S^2-]_min = K_sp(CuS) / [Cu^2+] = 10^(-36) / 0.01 = 10^(-34) M => [H^+]_max = sqrt(10^(-21)/10^(-34)) = 10^(6.5) M (satisfied at any pH > -6.5).
Maximum [S^2-] before ZnS precipitates: [S^2-]_max = K_sp(ZnS) / [Zn^2+] = 10^(-22) / 0.01 = 10^(-20) M.

sections.heading: Galvanic Cells, Electrochemical Series & Non-Additivity of E deg
sections.summary: A galvanic cell converts spontaneous chemical free energy (Delta G = -n F E_cell < 0) into electrical work with oxidation at the anode (negative terminal) and reduction at the cathode (positive terminal). Standard Reduction Potentials (SRP) rank oxidizing and reducing strengths relative to SHE (0.00 V).
keyPoints: Cell representation: Anode | Anode ion (C1) || Cathode ion (C2) | Cathode (double bar || is salt bridge with KCl, KNO3, or NH4NO3 — same ionic mobility of K^+ and Cl^- prevents liquid junction potential; avoid KCl with Ag^+/Pb^2+/Hg2^2+!).

EMF rule: E deg_cell = E deg_cathode(SRP) - E deg_anode(SRP). Higher SRP -> stronger OXIDIZING agent (F2 +2.87 V strongest; Li^+ -3.05 V weakest, so Li metal is strongest REDUCING agent in aqueous solution due to high hydration enthalpy!).
Non-additivity rule: E deg is INTENSIVE, so NEVER add or subtract half-cell potentials directly! Convert to Delta G deg = -n F E deg => E3 deg = (n1 E1 deg + n2 E2 deg) / n3.

Disproportionation (Latimer diagram): Intermediate species M^(n+) disproportionates spontaneously into M^((n+1)+) and M^((n-1)+) whenever E deg_right(reduction) > E deg_left(oxidation) (e.g., Cu^+ -> Cu^2+ + Cu; MnO4^2- in acid -> MnO4^- + MnO2).
Metal displacement & acid reaction: Any metal with E deg(M^(n+)/M) < 0 displaces H2 from dilute acids (Zn, Fe, Mg), whereas Cu (+0.34 V), Ag (+0.80 V), Au cannot!

sections.heading: Nernst Equation, Equilibrium Constant & Commercial Cells / Corrosion
sections.summary: The Nernst equation quantifies how non-standard concentrations and gas pressures alter cell potential until equilibrium (E_cell = 0, Q = K_c) is reached. Primary cells are non-rechargeable, whereas secondary cells and H2-O2 fuel cells reverse or continuously replenish electrode reactions.
keyPoints: Nernst Equation (at 298 K, 2.303 RT / F = 0.0591 V): E_cell = E deg_cell - (0.0591 / n) log10(Q); for single reduction half-cell M^(n+) + n e^- -> M: E = E deg - (0.0591 / n) log10(1 / [M^(n+)]).
Hydrogen electrode pH dependence: Pt | H2(1 bar) | H^+(pH) has E_red = -0.0591 * pH (and E_ox = +0.0591 * pH).
At chemical equilibrium: E_cell = 0 and Q = K_c => E deg_cell = (0.0591 / n) log10(K_c) (so K_c = 10^(n * E deg_cell / 0.0591)).

Primary Batteries: Leclanche Dry Cell (Zn anode, MnO2 + C cathode, NH4Cl + ZnCl2 paste, ~1.5 V); Mercury Button Cell (Zn-Hg anode, HgO + C cathode, KOH paste -> constant ~1.35 V throughout life because net reaction involves no dissolved ions!).

Secondary Batteries & Fuel Cell: Lead-Storage (Pb anode, PbO2 cathode, 38% H2SO4; discharging forms PbSO4 at BOTH electrodes and consumes H2SO4; recharging reverses); Ni-Cd (longer life); H2-O2 Fuel Cell (~70% efficiency, porous C + Pt/Pd, hot aq KOH, 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O).

Rusting of Iron (electrochemical): Anode Fe -> Fe^2+ + 2e^-; Cathode O2 + 4H^+ + 4e^- -> 2 H2O; overall Fe2O3.xH2O. Prevented by sacrificial anodic protection using more electropositive Mg or Zn (galvanization).

sections.heading: Electrolytic Cells, Faraday's Laws & Product Overpotential
sections.summary: Electrolysis drives non-spontaneous redox processes using external DC voltage (anode is positive, cathode is negative), depositing mass strictly proportional to passed charge Q = I * t. In aqueous solutions, competing water oxidation/reduction and bubble overpotentials govern actual electrode products.
keyPoints: Faraday's First Law: Mass deposited w = Z * Q = (M * I * t) / (n * 96500), where 1 Faraday = 96487 ~= 96500 C/mol e^- deposits exactly 1 gram-equivalent.
Faraday's Second Law (cells in series with identical Q): w1 / E_eq1 = w2 / E_eq2, or moles deposited n_1 * z_1 = n_2 * z_2.
Cathode preference (higher SRP reduces first): K^+, Na^+, Ca^2+, Mg^2+, Al^3+ stay in water -> H2O reduces to H2(g) + 2 OH^-! Cu^2+, Ag^+, Au^3+ reduce preferentially over H2O.

Anode preference (lower SRP oxidizes first, WITH O2 overpotential): F^-, SO4^2-, NO3^- NEVER oxidize in water -> H2O oxidizes to O2(g) + 4 H^+! In conc. aq NaCl, Cl^- oxidizes to Cl2(g) instead of O2 due to high oxygen overvoltage on Pt/graphite; in very dilute NaCl, O2 evolves!

Electrolysis of dil. H2SO4 -> H2 (cathode) + O2 (anode, 2:1 volume); conc. H2SO4 (high current density) -> H2 + H2S2O8 (peroxydisulphuric acid); aq CuSO4 with Inert Pt -> Cu + O2 (pH drops!), with Cu electrodes -> Cu dissolves at anode & deposits at cathode.

sections.heading: Conductance, Kohlrausch's Law & Conductometric Titrations
sections.summary: Ionic conductance increases with temperature (lower solvent viscosity) and follows Kohlrausch's law of independent ionic migration at infinite dilution. Upon diluting any electrolyte, specific conductivity kappa drops (fewer ions per mL) while molar conductivity Lambda_m rises.
keyPoints: Definitions: Conductance G = 1/R (S or Ohm^(-1)); Specific conductivity kappa = G * (l/A) = G * G* (S/cm); Molar conductivity Lambda_m = (1000 * kappa) / M (S.cm^2/mol) = kappa / C (in SI S.m^2/mol when C in mol/m^3); Lambda_eq = Lambda_m / n-factor.

Dilution contrast: kappa ALWAYS decreases on dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes; Lambda_m increases slowly for strong electrolytes (Debye-Huckel-Onsager Lambda_m = Lambda_m deg - A sqrt(C)) and shoots up steeply near C -> 0 for weak electrolytes!
Kohlrausch's Law: Lambda_m deg(A_x B_y) = x * lambda deg(A^(y+)) + y * lambda deg(B^(x-)). Indirectly finds Lambda_m deg(CH3COOH) = Lambda deg(CH3COONa) + Lambda deg(HCl) - Lambda deg(NaCl).
Applications: Degree of ionization alpha = Lambda_m / Lambda_m deg; Ka = (C * alpha^2) / (1 - alpha); Solubility of sparingly soluble AgCl S = (1000 * kappa_salt) / Lambda_m deg(AgCl).

Conductometric Titrations: Fast H^+ (349.8) and OH^- (198 S.cm^2/mol) dominate slopes! SA+SB gives sharp V-shape; WA+SB drops slightly, rises slowly (salt buffer), then shoots up after equivalence; WB+SA rises slowly then shoots up; WA+WB rises then flattens cleanly!

sections.heading: Chemical Kinetics: Rate Laws, Molecularity & Integrated Orders
sections.summary: Reaction rate equals (-1/nu_A) d[A]/dt for reactants and (+1/nu_P) d[P]/dt for products, while experimental rate laws Rate = k [A]^x [B]^y determine overall order (x + y). Molecularity applies strictly to elementary steps and is always a positive integer (1, 2, or rarely 3).
keyPoints: Zero Order: [A] = [A]_0 - k t; t_1/2 = [A]_0 / (2k); t_100% = [A]_0 / k (finishes in finite time!). Examples: NH3 decomposition on hot Pt/W, HI on Au at high pressure, photochemical H2 + Cl2.

First Order: k = (2.303 / t) log([A]_0 / [A]); t_1/2 = 0.693 / k (independent of [A]_0!); t_75% = 2 t_1/2, t_87.5% = 3 t_1/2, t_99% = 6.64 t_1/2, t_99.9% = 10 t_1/2. Examples: radioactive decay, N2O5 decomposition, H2O2 decomposition.
Pseudo-First Order: Bimolecular reaction with one reactant in huge excess (H2O in acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis or cane-sugar inversion) behaves as 1st order with k_obs = k'[H2O].

First-order indirect metrics: Gas A(g) -> B(g) + C(g): k = (2.303/t) log[P_i / (2 P_i - P_t)]; H2O2 vs KMnO4 titration: log(V_0 / V_t); Cane sugar polarimetry: log[(r_0 - r_inf) / (r_t - r_inf)]; Ester hydrolysis with NaOH: log[(V_inf - V_0) / (V_inf - V_t)].
General nth order (n != 1): k t = [1/(n - 1)] * (1/[A]^(n-1) - 1/[A]_0^(n-1)); t_1/2 proportional to [A]_0^(1 - n).

sections.heading: Complex Kinetics, Arrhenius Equation & Collision Theory
sections.summary: Multi-step mechanisms combine parallel, sequential, or reversible elementary steps analyzed via steady-state approximation (d[Intermediate]/dt = 0). Arrhenius theory connects rate constant exponentially to activation energy E_a, which catalysts lower equally for forward and reverse steps.
keyPoints: Parallel First Order (A -> B with k1, A -> C with k2): k_eff = k1 + k2; t_1/2 = 0.693 / (k1 + k2); Product ratio [B]/[C] = k1 / k2; Effective E_a = (k1 E_a1 + k2 E_a2) / (k1 + k2).
Sequential First Order (A -k1-> B -k2-> C): [B] peaks at t_max = ln(k2/k1) / (k2 - k1); if k1 << k2 (Step 1 RDS), overall rate ~= k1 [A].
Reversible First Order (A <-> B, k_f, k_b): (k_f + k_b) t = ln([A]_0 - [A]_eq) / ([A] - [A]_eq), and K_eq = k_f / k_b.

Arrhenius Equation: k = A * e^(-E_a / R T) => log10(k2 / k1) = (E_a / 2.303 R) * (1/T1 - 1/T2). At T -> infinity, k -> A (pre-exponential frequency factor). Rule of thumb: rate doubles/triples per 10 K rise.
Enthalpy & Catalyst effect: Delta H_rxn = E_a(forward) - E_a(backward). Catalyst lowers BOTH E_a(f) and E_a(b) by the exact same amount -> Delta H, Delta G, and K_eq remain UNCHANGED!
Collision Theory: k = P * Z_AB * e^(-E_a / R T), where P is steric/orientation probability factor and e^(-E_a/RT) is fraction of molecules with kinetic energy >= E_a.

solvedExamples.question: Given E deg(Cu^2+/Cu) = +0.34 V and E deg(Cu^+/Cu) = +0.52 V, calculate E deg(Cu^2+/Cu^+) and check if Cu^+ disproportionates in aqueous solution.
steps: Write target half-cell: (3) Cu^2+ + 1e^- -> Cu^+, obtained from (1) Cu^2+ + 2e^- -> Cu (E1 = +0.34 V, n1 = 2) MINUS (2) Cu^+ + 1e^- -> Cu (E2 = +0.52 V, n2 = 1).
Apply Delta G3 deg = Delta G1 deg - Delta G2 deg => -1*F*E3 = -2*F*(0.34) - (-1*F*(0.52)).
Check disproportionation 2 Cu^+ -> Cu^2+ + Cu: E deg_cell = E deg(Cu^+/Cu) - E deg(Cu^2+/Cu^+) = 0.52 - 0.16 = +0.36 V > 0 => YES, Cu^+ disproportionates!
solvedExamples.answer: E deg(Cu^2+/Cu^+) = +0.16 V; Cu^+ spontaneously disproportionates
solvedExamples.pitfall: Subtracting 0.34 - 0.52 = -0.18 V without multiplying by electron counts n1, n2.

solvedExamples.question: The molar conductivity of 0.025 mol/L methanoic acid (HCOOH) is 46.1 S.cm^2/mol. Calculate its degree of dissociation and K_a given lambda deg(H^+) = 349.6 and lambda deg(HCOO^-) = 54.6 S.cm^2/mol.
steps: By Kohlrausch's law: Lambda_m deg(HCOOH) = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2 S.cm^2/mol.
Degree of dissociation alpha = Lambda_m / Lambda_m deg = 46.1 / 404.2 = 0.114 (11.4%).
Since alpha > 0.05, use exact Ostwald formula: K_a = (C * alpha^2) / (1 - alpha).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Dropping (1 - alpha) in the denominator when alpha = 11.4% (> 5%) introduces >12% error!

solvedExamples.question: The rate constant of a reaction increases by a factor of 4 when temperature is raised from 293 K to 313 K. Calculate activation energy E_a (R = 8.314 J/mol.K, log10(2) = 0.3010).
steps: Use Arrhenius two-temperature form: log10(k2 / k1) = (E_a / 2.303 R) * [(T2 - T1) / (T1 * T2)].
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using temperatures in Celsius (20 C and 40 C) instead of Kelvin (293 K and 313 K)!

solvedExamples.question: For a parallel first-order decomposition of A into B (k1 = 2 x 10^(-3) s^(-1), E_a1 = 40 kJ/mol) and C (k2 = 6 x 10^(-3) s^(-1), E_a2 = 80 kJ/mol), find the overall half-life of A, mole fraction of B in products, and effective activation energy.
steps: Overall rate of disappearance: -d[A]/dt = (k1 + k2)[A] => k_eff = 2e-3 + 6e-3 = 8 x 10^(-3) s^(-1).
Product branching ratio [B] / ([B] + [C]) = k1 / (k1 + k2) = 2 / 8 = 0.25 (25% B, 75% C).

sections.heading: p-Block Groups 13 & 14: Inert Pair Effect, Anomalies, Halides & Allotropes
sections.summary: Down Groups 13 and 14, poor shielding by inner d and f electrons raises Z_eff on outer ns^2 electrons (inert pair effect), stabilizing lower oxidation states (+1 in Tl, +2 in Pb) over group valency. Second-period B and C show maximum covalency 4 and strong ppi-ppi multiple bonding unlike heavier congeners.
keyPoints: Group 13 trends: IE1 B > Tl > Ga > Al > In; Radius B < Ga < Al < In < Tl; +1 stability B < Al < Ga < In < Tl (Tl^+ > Tl^3+, so TlI3 is actually Tl^+ I3^-!).

Group 13 halides & oxides: BF3 < BCl3 < BBr3 < BI3 Lewis acidity; AlCl3 dimerizes (Al2Cl6, 3c-4e Cl bridges) in vapour/non-polar solvents and dissolves in water forming [Al(H2O)6]^3+; B2O3 acidic, Al2O3/Ga2O3 amphoteric, In2O3/Tl2O basic.
Group 14 inert pair & halides: C >> Si > Ge ~= Sn >> Pb catenation; Pb^2+ > Pb^4+ (PbO2 is strong oxidant; PbCl4 decomposes, PbI4 does NOT exist!); GeX2 < SnX2 < PbX2 stability.

Hydrolysis & oxides: CCl4 does NOT hydrolyze (no d-orbitals), whereas SiCl4 hydrolyzes violently to Si(OH)4 + 4 HCl. CO2 is linear discrete gas (sp), while SiO2 is high-melting 3D covalent network (sp3 SiO4 tetrahedra).

Carbon allotropes: Diamond (sp3, 3D tetrahedral, insulator, hardest); Graphite (sp2 hexagonal sheets, delocalized pi e- conductor, thermodynamic delta_f H = 0, soft lubricant); Fullerene C60 (sp2, 20 hexagons + 12 pentagons, zero dangling bonds!).

sections.heading: p-Block Groups 15, 16, 17 & 18: Hydrides, Oxoacids & Xenon Compounds
sections.summary: N2, O2, and F2 exhibit anomalous small-size high-EN behaviour, strong ppi-ppi bonding, and low single-bond energy (N-N < P-P, O-O < S-S, F-F < Cl-Cl) due to lone-pair repulsion. Oxoacid basicity equals the exact count of -OH protons attached to the central atom.
keyPoints: Group 15 hydrides & P oxoacids: BP BiH3 > SbH3 > NH3 > AsH3 > PH3; Thermal stability & Basicity NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3 > BiH3; Reducing power increases down! P oxoacids: H3PO2 (1 -OH, 2 P-H: monobasic strong reducer), H3PO3 (2 -OH, 1 P-H: dibasic reducer -> disproportionates on heating to H3PO4 + PH3), H3PO4 (3 -OH: tribasic), H4P2O7 (4 -OH), (HPO3)3 cyclic.

Halide hydrolysis contrast: NCl3 + 3 H2O -> NH3 + 3 HOCl (lone pair attack on Cl), whereas PCl3 + 3 H2O -> H3PO3 + 3 HCl; PCl5 -> POCl3 -> H3PO4. Bi^5+ (NaBiO3) is an ultra-strong oxidant (inert pair Bi^3+ > Bi^5+).

Group 16 hydrides & S oxoacids: BP H2O >> H2Te > H2Se > H2S; Acidic strength & Reducing power H2O < H2S < H2Se < H2Te. O-O BDE < S-S, so S forms S8 crown; S2 vapour at high T is paramagnetic like O2! H2SO5 (1 peroxo), H2S2O8 (1 peroxo), H2S2O7 oleum (S-O-S), H2S2O3 (S-S).

Group 17 Halogens: Oxidizing power F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 (F2 high hydration & low F-F BDE!); BDE order Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2; Aqueous acid strength HF < HCl < HBr < HI (weak H-F breaks hardest!). Oxoacids: HOCl < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4 (acidic strength & thermal stability both rise with oxidation state!). Interhalogens XX' (ClF), XX'3 (ClF3 T-shaped), XX'5 (BrF5), XX'7 (IF7) are more reactive than X2 except F2!

Group 18 Noble Gases: IE1 Ne > Ar > Kr > Xe > Rn (Xe ~= O2 = 1170 kJ/mol -> Bartlett's Xe^+[PtF6]^-). XeF2 (sp3d linear) + H2O -> Xe + HF + O2; 6 XeF4 + 12 H2O -> 4 Xe + 2 XeO3 + 24 HF + 3 O2 (disproportionation!); XeF6 partial hydrolysis -> XeOF4 -> XeO2F2 -> XeO3 (pyramidal explosive!).

sections.heading: d-Block Transition Elements: Electronic, Magnetic & Redox Trends
sections.summary: Transition metals (partially filled d-orbitals in ground or common oxidation state, excluding d^10 Zn, Cd, Hg) showcase variable oxidation states, paramagnetism, coloured hydrated ions, catalytic activity, and interstitial alloys. 4d and 5d metals strongly favor higher oxidation states unlike 3d elements.
keyPoints: Non-transition d-block: Zn, Cd, Hg (full d^10 in 0 and +2) show low enthalpy of atomization, soft/volatile nature (Hg liquid), and diamagnetic colourless salts.
Melting point & atomization peak: Highest near d^5 (Cr, Mo, W — W highest MP among metals!); Mn & Tc show anomalous dips in MP due to stable half-filled 3d^5 weakening metallic bonding!
IE & Radius trends: IE3 jumps sharply at Mn^2+ (3d^5 -> 3d^4) and Fe^3+ stability. Radii shrink Sc -> Cr, plateau Mn -> Ni, and expand at Cu -> Zn.

Standard Electrode Potentials E deg(M^2+/M): Only Cu is POSITIVE (+0.34 V) due to high atomization + IE1+IE2 exceeding hydration enthalpy! E deg(M^3+/M^2+): Sc^3+ ultra-stable (very negative), Mn^3+/Mn^2+ (+1.57 V) & Co^3+/Co^2+ (+1.97 V) strongly oxidizing, Cr^2+/Cr^3+ (-0.41 V) strongly reducing (Cr^2+ d^4 -> Cr^3+ t2g^3 half-filled!).

Highest oxidation states stabilized by O & F (e.g. Mn2O7 covalent green oil, CrO3, V2O5, OsO4; F stabilizes up to MnF4 while O reaches Mn2O7 via ppi-dpi double bonds!). Cu^2+ + 4 I^- -> Cu2I2(white) + I2 (CuI2 decomposes!).
Interstitial compounds (TiC, Mn4N, Fe3H): retain metallic conductivity, higher MP, harder, chemically inert. Catalysts: Fe (Haber), V2O5 (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), TiCl4 + AlEt3 (Ziegler-Natta).

sections.heading: K2Cr2O7, KMnO4 & f-Block (Lanthanoids + Actinoids)
sections.summary: Potassium dichromate and permanganate serve as flagship transition-metal oxidants whose products and colours shift cleanly with pH. Across the 4f and 5f series, lanthanoid and actinoid contractions narrow atomic radii while actinoids access much wider oxidation states due to comparable 5f, 6d, and 7s energies.
keyPoints: K2Cr2O7 preparation: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4) + Na2CO3 + O2 -> Na2CrO4 (yellow) + H2SO4 -> Na2Cr2O7 + KCl -> K2Cr2O7 (orange). pH equilibrium: 2 CrO4^2- (yellow, Td) + 2 H^+ <=> Cr2O7^2- (orange, two corner-shared Td with Cr-O-Cr angle 126 deg) + H2O.
K2Cr2O7 oxidations (acidic, n=6 -> Cr^3+ green): oxidizes I^- -> I2, Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+, H2S -> S, SO2 -> SO4^2-, Sn^2+ -> Sn^4+. With H2O2 in acid forms deep blue CrO5 (stabilized in ether!).

KMnO4 preparation: Pyrolusite (MnO2) + KOH + O2 -> K2MnO4 (dark green, paramagnetic 1e-) -> electrolytic oxidation or disproportionation in acid/CO2 -> KMnO4 (dark purple, diamagnetic charge-transfer!).

KMnO4 medium sensitivity: Acidic (n=5 -> Mn^2+ colourless): oxidizes C2O4^2- (autocatalyzed by Mn^2+), Fe^2+, NO2^-, SO3^2-, I^- -> I2. Neutral/faintly alkaline (n=3 -> MnO2 brown ppt): oxidizes I^- -> IO3^- (iodate!), S2O3^2- -> SO4^2-, Mn^2+ -> MnO2! Strongly alkaline (n=1): MnO4^2-.

Lanthanoids (4f, Ce 58 to Lu 71): Common +3 state; exceptions Ce^4+ (4f^0, strong oxidant, analytical titrant), Eu^2+ (4f^7) & Yb^2+ (4f^14) strong reductants! Hydroxide basicity La(OH)3 > ... > Lu(OH)3 (Fajan's rule!). Mischmetall (95% Ln + 5% Fe).
Actinoids (5f, Th 90 to Lr 103): Radioactive; access +3 to +7 (Np, Pu reach +7!) because 5f, 6d, 7s levels are nearly degenerate; 5f shielding is even poorer than 4f -> steeper actinoid contraction.

sections.heading: Coordination Compounds: Werner's Theory, IUPAC Naming & Isomerism
sections.summary: Werner distinguished ionizable primary valency (oxidation state) from directional, non-ionizable secondary valency (coordination number), explaining precipitation stoichiometry and stereochemistry. Structural and stereoisomerism give rise to predictable geometrical and optically active counts.
keyPoints: Double salts (Mohr's salt FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, Carnallite, Alum) dissociate completely into simple ions; Coordination complexes ([Fe(CN)6]^4-) retain complex ion identity in water.

Ligand types: Monodentate (NH3, H2O, CO, CN^-, X^-), Bidentate (en, ox^2-, gly^-), Hexadentate (EDTA^4- -> forms 5 chelate rings!), Ambidentate (NO2^-/ONO^-, SCN^-/NCS^-, CN^-/NC^-). Chelate effect boosts thermodynamic stability (Delta S > 0!).

IUPAC Rules: Cation before anion; inside bracket list ligands ALPHABETICALLY before central metal; anionic complex ends in '-ate' with Roman oxidation state; use bis/tris/tetrakis for polydentate or prefix-containing ligands (e.g. tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III)); bridging ligands use mu-.

Structural Isomerism: Ionization ([Co(NH3)5SO4]Br vs [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4), Solvate/Hydrate ([Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 violet vs [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O blue-green vs [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.2H2O dark green), Linkage (ambidentate), Coordination ([Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6]).

Geometrical Isomerism: Square planar Ma2b2 (cis-platin anticancer! vs trans), Mabcd (3 GI); Tetrahedral shows ZERO GI (Wait: Mabcd tetrahedral IS optically active!); Octahedral Ma4b2 (2), Ma3b3 (fac vs mer = 2), M(AA)2a2 (2 GI -> cis is optically active = 3 total stereoisomers), Ma2b2c2 (5 GI -> 6 total stereoisomers), Mabcdef (15 GI -> 30 stereoisomers!).
Optical Isomerism: Chiral octahedrals lacking POS/COS -> [M(AA)3] (d,l pair, e.g. [Co(en)3]^3+), cis-[M(AA)2a2], cis-[M(AA)2ab], [M(AB)3] (2 GI fac/mer, BOTH optically active -> 4 total!).

sections.heading: Coordination Bonding: VBT, Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Jahn-Teller & Carbonyls
sections.summary: Crystal Field Theory models d-orbital electrostatic splitting by ligands into t2g and eg levels (Delta_o in octahedral, Delta_t = 4/9 Delta_o in tetrahedral), predicting spin state, magnetic moment, CFSE, and d-d absorption colours. Metal carbonyls stabilize low/zero oxidation states via synergic sigma-donation and pi*-back-bonding.
keyPoints: VBT classics: [Fe(CN)6]^4- (d2sp3 inner Oh, 0 e- diamag) vs [FeF6]^3- (sp3d2 outer Oh, 5 e- 5.92 BM); [Ni(CN)4]^2- (dsp2 sq planar, diamag) vs [NiCl4]^2- (sp3 Td, 2 e- 2.83 BM) vs Ni(CO)4 (sp3 Td, diamag!); [CoF6]^3- (sp3d2, 4 e-) vs [Co(NH3)6]^3+ (d2sp3, 0 e-).
Spectrochemical Series (weak -> strong): I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < S^2- < F^- < OH^- < C2O4^2- < H2O < NCS^- < EDTA^4- < NH3 < en < CN^- < CO.

Octahedral CFSE & pairing: CFSE = (-0.4 n_t2g + 0.6 n_eg) Delta_o + m*P. Strong field (Delta_o > P) pairs d^4-d^7 into t2g first; Weak field (Delta_o < P) fills eg before pairing. Note Co^3+ (d^6) has high charge so even H2O & C2O4^2- act strong-field -> [Co(H2O)6]^3+ and [Co(ox)3]^3- are DIAMAGNETIC!
Tetrahedral complexes: e (lower) and t2 (higher), Delta_t = (4/9) Delta_o < P ALWAYS => tetrahedral complexes are virtually ALWAYS high spin!

Jahn-Teller Distortion: Unequal occupation of eg orbitals causes strong axial elongation/compression -> strongly seen in d^9 (Cu^2+: 2 long axial, 4 short eq bonds), HS d^4 (Cr^2+, Mn^3+), and LS d^7!

Colour & Carbonyls: d^0 (Ti^4+, Sc^3+) & d^10 (Zn^2+, Cu^+) are colourless (except MnO4^-, CrO4^2-, Cr2O7^2- via ligand-to-metal charge transfer!). [Ti(H2O)6]^3+ is purple. In M-CO carbonyls, M -> CO(pi*) back-bonding strengthens M-C bond and WEAKENS C-O bond (lowers C-O stretching frequency; Sidgwick EAN = 36/54/86 in Fe(CO)5, Cr(CO)6, Ni(CO)4, Mn2(CO)10).

steps: For [Fe(CN)6]^3-: IUPAC = Hexacyanidoferrate(III) ion. Fe is +3 (3d^5); CN^- is strong-field -> low-spin t2g^5 eg^0 (2 pairings beyond 1 already paired? Wait: 5 e- in weak field = 0 pairs; in strong field = 2 pairs -> m = 2).
Hybridization = d2sp3 (inner orbital octahedral); unpaired e- n = 1 => mu = sqrt(1*3) = 1.73 BM; CFSE = 5(-0.4) Delta_o + 2P = -2.0 Delta_o + 2P.
For [Co(C2O4)3]^3-: IUPAC = Tris(oxalato)cobaltate(III) ion. Co is +3 (3d^6); with Co^3+, oxalate acts as strong-field -> t2g^6 eg^0 (d2sp3, diamagnetic n = 0 => mu = 0 BM).
Weak-field d^6 has 1 pair; strong-field t2g^6 has 3 pairs => delta pairing = 2P; CFSE = 6(-0.4) Delta_o + 2P = -2.4 Delta_o + 2P.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Treating [Co(C2O4)3]^3- as high-spin paramagnetic like [CoF6]^3-!

solvedExamples.question: Arrange the following in increasing order of C-O bond length: CO, [Fe(CO)5], [Mn(CO)6]^+, [V(CO)6]^-.
steps: In metal carbonyls, higher negative charge on the metal enhances M -> CO(pi*) synergic back-bonding.
Back-bonding populates the antibonding pi* orbital of CO, decreasing C-O bond order and lengthening the C-O bond.
Charge density on metal: [V(CO)6]^- (-1) > [Fe(CO)5] (0) > [Mn(CO)6]^+ (+1); free CO has zero back-bonding (BO = 3.0).
Therefore C-O bond length order: CO < [Mn(CO)6]^+ < [Fe(CO)5] < [V(CO)6]^-.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Thinking stronger M-C bonding also strengthens C-O — they move in OPPOSITE directions!

solvedExamples.question: How many moles of KMnO4 are required in neutral or faintly alkaline medium to oxidize 1 mole of KI completely, and what is the manganese-containing product?
steps: In neutral/faintly alkaline medium, MnO4^- reduces to brown MnO2 (Mn +7 -> +4, n-factor = 3).
Crucial NCERT reaction: I^- is oxidized to iodate IO3^- (I -1 -> +5, n-factor = 6), NOT I2!
Equate equivalents: n(KMnO4) * 3 = 1 * 6 => n(KMnO4) = 2 moles.
Balanced reaction: 2 MnO4^- + H2O + I^- -> 2 MnO2 + 2 OH^- + IO3^-.
solvedExamples.answer: 2 moles of KMnO4; product is MnO2 (and IO3^-)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming I^- always oxidizes to I2 (acidic medium rule) gives wrong answer 1/3 mole!

solvedExamples.question: Count the total number of geometrical isomers and total stereoisomers for (i) [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3], (ii) [Pt(gly)2], (iii) [Co(en)2ClBr]^+, and (iv) [Cr(NH3)2Cl2Br2]^-.
steps: (i) [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3] is Ma3b3: has 2 geometrical isomers (facial and meridional), both possess symmetry planes => 0 optical => 2 stereoisomers total.
(ii) [Pt(gly)2] is square planar M(AB)2 with unsymmetrical bidentate glycinate: has 2 geometrical isomers (cis and trans), both planar => 2 stereoisomers total.
(iii) [Co(en)2ClBr]^+ is M(AA)2ab: has 2 geometrical isomers (cis and trans). Trans has symmetry plane (1); Cis is chiral and splits into d,l enantiomeric pair (2) => 3 stereoisomers total.
(iv) [Cr(NH3)2Cl2Br2]^- is Ma2b2c2: has 5 geometrical isomers (all-trans, 3x one-trans-two-cis, all-cis). Only the all-cis isomer is chiral (d,l pair) => 5 GI and 6 stereoisomers total!
solvedExamples.answer: (i) 2 GI, 2 stereo; (ii) 2 GI, 2 stereo; (iii) 2 GI, 3 stereo; (iv) 5 GI, 6 stereo
solvedExamples.pitfall: Missing the chiral all-cis enantiomeric pair in Ma2b2c2 gives 5 instead of 6 stereoisomers.

sections.heading: IUPAC Nomenclature, DBE & Conformational Isomerism
sections.summary: Systematic IUPAC naming prioritizes principal functional groups (-COOH > -SO3H > anhydrides > esters > -COCl > -CONH2 > -CN > -CHO > >C=O > -OH > -NH2 > C=C/C#C > halo/nitro/alkoxy) and lowest locant sets. Conformational isomers interconvert rapidly by sigma-bond rotation, minimizing torsional and van der Waals strain.
keyPoints: Degree of Unsaturation (DBE): DBE = C + 1 - (H + X - N)/2 (ignore divalent O, S). Each ring or pi bond = +1; C#C = +2; Benzene = 4.

Structural Isomers: Chain, Position, Functional (alcohol/ether, aldehyde/ketone, acid/ester, 1/2/3 deg amines, cyanide/isocyanide), Metamerism (different alkyl chains on divalent -O-/-S-/-NH-/-COO-), Ring-chain.

Keto-Enol Tautomerism: Requires alpha-H on sp3 carbon (or gamma-H in conjugated systems). Enol % increases via intramolecular H-bonding & conjugation: Acetone (~0.0001%) < Ethyl acetoacetate (~7%) < Acetylacetone (~76%) < Phenol (~100% aromaticity!).
Butane Newman Conformations (C2-C3): Anti (180 deg, lowest energy) > Gauche (60 deg, ~3.8 kJ/mol higher) > Partially Eclipsed (120 deg) > Fully Eclipsed (0 deg, ~19 kJ/mol highest).

Gauche Stability Exception: Ethylene glycol (HO-CH2-CH2-OH), 2-fluoroethanol, and 2-aminoethanol stabilize Gauche OVER Anti via intramolecular H-bonding (or hyperconjugation gauche effect in 1,2-difluoroethane!).
Cyclohexane Chair: Equatorial substituents avoid 1,3-diaxial steric repulsion (tert-butyl locks completely equatorial!). Chair-to-chair ring flip swaps ALL axial <-> equatorial positions.

sections.heading: Geometrical (E/Z) & Optical Stereochemistry (R/S, Meso & Atropisomerism)
sections.summary: Geometrical isomerism arises from restricted rotation about C=C, C=N (oximes), N=N, or cycloalkane rings whenever each terminal carries two distinct groups. Optical activity requires molecular chirality (absence of plane, centre, and alternating axis of symmetry).
keyPoints: CIP Priority Rules: Higher atomic number atom on directly bonded carbon wins (I > Br > Cl > S > P > F > O > N > C > D > H); break ties atom-by-atom outward; expand C=O as C-(O)(O) and C#N as C-(N)(N)(N). E = entgegen (high priorities opposite); Z = zusammen (same side).

Minimum ring size for trans-cycloalkene stability at room temp: Cyclooctene (C8); cyclohexene & cycloheptene exist only as cis! Cumulenes: even C=C bonds (allenes a,b-C=C=C-a,b) show OPTICAL isomerism (no POS/COS!); odd C=C bonds show GEOMETRICAL isomerism!

R/S Assignment: Place lowest priority (#4) away (vertical in Fischer or dashed wedge) -> 1->2->3 clockwise = R, counterclockwise = S. If #4 sits on horizontal Fischer or solid wedge, FLIP result (R <-> S)!

Symmetry & Meso Compounds: 2,3-dichlorobutane or tartaric acid has 2 identical chiral centres -> 1 Meso (optically inactive by internal compensation: POS/COS present) + 1 d/l enantiomeric pair = 3 stereoisomers (NOT 4!).

Stereoisomer relations: Enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images, identical BP/MP, opposite optical rotation); Diastereomers (non-mirror stereoisomers, different BP/MP/solubility -> separable by fractional distillation/crystallization!); Racemic mixture (50:50 d+l, opt. inactive by external compensation).
Atropisomerism: Bulky ortho-tetrasubstituted biphenyls restrict C-C single-bond rotation, keeping two phenyl rings perpendicular and optically active (if each ring is unsymmetrically substituted).

sections.heading: Electronic Effects (+I/+M/Hyperconjugation), Bredt's Rule & Aromaticity
sections.summary: Permanent electronic displacements (Inductive sigma-pull, Resonance pi-delocalization, Hyperconjugation sigma-p overlap) govern intermediate stability and reactivity. Huckel's (4n + 2) pi rule identifies planar cyclic aromatic systems with massive resonance stabilization.
keyPoints: Inductive orders: -I: -NF3^+ > -NR3^+ > -SR2^+ > -NH3^+ > -NO2 > -SO3H > -CN > -CHO > -COOH > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I > -OR > -OH > -C#CH > -NH2 > -Ph; +I: -O^- > -COO^- > 3 deg R > 2 deg R > 1 deg R > -CH3 > -T > -D > -H.

Mesomeric (+M / -M): +M: -O^- > -NH2 > -NHR > -NR2 > -OH > -OR > -NHCOR > -OCOR > -Ph > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I; -M: -NO2 > -CN > -CHO > -COR > -COOH > -COOR > -CONH2. Resonance ALWAYS dominates Inductive except in halogens (-I > +M for reactivity, +M > -I for orientation!).

Hyperconjugation (no-bond resonance): Stabilizes carbocations, free radicals, and alkenes proportionally to alpha-H count! Heat of hydrogenation (lower = more stable alkene) drops as alkyl substitution on C=C rises; C-H bond breaks slightly faster than C-D (Baker-Nathan / isotope effect).
Bredt's Rule: A double bond (or sp2 carbocation) CANNOT be placed at the bridgehead carbon of small bicyclic systems (e.g. bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) because orbital orthogonality prevents pi-overlap!

Huckel Aromaticity (cyclic, planar, complete conjugation): (4n+2) pi = Aromatic (Benzene, Naphthalene 10, Anthracene 14, C5H5^- 6, C7H7^+ tropylium 6, cyclopropenyl cation 2, Pyridine/Pyrrole/Furan/Thiophene 6, [18]annulene); 4n pi = Anti-aromatic (C4H4 cyclobutadiene, C5H5^+, C3H3^-, C8H8 planar -> C8H8 adopts tub non-aromatic shape!).

Quasi-aromatic & Homoaromatic: Tropolone, azulene (high dipole moment ~1 D!), squaric acid dianion gain aromaticity via ionic resonance; homotropylium ion (C8H9^+) is homoaromatic (6 pi across a CH2 bridge).

sections.heading: Reaction Intermediates, Carbocation Rearrangements & Acid-Base Strength
sections.summary: Carbocations rearrange spontaneously via 1,2-hydride, 1,2-methyl, or ring-expansion shifts whenever a more stable cation forms, whereas carbanions and radicals resist simple 1,2 shifts. Acidity and basicity depend on conjugate stability, steric inhibition of resonance (SIR), and solvation.
keyPoints: Carbocation stability: Cyclopropylmethyl cations ((c-Pr)3C^+ > (c-Pr)2CH^+ > Ph3C^+ > Ph2CH^+ > Allyl ~ 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg > Vinyl ~ Phenyl!).
Ring expansion & contraction: 3-membered -> 4-membered (or cyclopropylmethyl equilibrium); 4-membered -> 5-membered; 5-membered -> 6-membered whenever positive charge sits adjacent to ring!

Carbenes (:CH2): Singlet (sp2, paired e- in sp2 + vacant p, bent ~103 deg, stereospecific syn-addition to alkenes); Triplet (sp, 2 unpaired e-, linear/wide ~136 deg, MORE stable, non-stereospecific radical addition).
Acidity order: RSO3H > Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) > HCOOH > PhCOOH > RCOOH > H2CO3 > Phenol > H2O > ROH (MeOH > EtOH > i-PrOH > t-BuOH!) > HC#CH > NH3 > RCH=CH2 > RH.

Ortho Effect (Benzoic Acids): ALMOST ANY ortho substituent (-OH, -NO2, -Cl, -CH3, -OCH3) twists -COOH out of ring plane, blocking +M donation from ring and raising steric hydration of -COO^- -> makes o-substituted benzoic acid STRONGER than benzoic acid! (o-hydroxybenzoic pKa 2.98 << m/p).

Basicity & SIR/SIP: Guanidine > Amidine > Aliphatic amines > NH3 > Aniline > Pyridine (sp2 lp localized) > Pyrrole (lp part of 6 pi aromatic ring -> non-basic!). In o-substituted anilines/N,N-dimethylanilines, SIR weakens protonation (o-methylaniline weakest, EXCEPT 2,6-dimethyl-N,N-dimethylaniline is STRONGER base because -NMe2 twists out and loses delocalization into ring!).

sections.heading: Alkanes & Alkenes: Preparation, Regioselectivity & Stereospecific Additions
sections.summary: Alkanes react primarily via free-radical substitution (where Br2 is far more selective than Cl2 for 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg C-H), whereas alkenes undergo electrophilic additions whose regioselectivity and syn/anti stereochemistry are controlled precisely by reagent mechanism.
keyPoints: Alkane synthesis: Wurtz (2 R-X + 2 Na/dry ether -> symmetrical R-R, fails for 3 deg halides -> elimination!), Corey-House (R2CuLi + R'-X -> unsymmetrical alkanes cleanly!), Kolbe electrolysis (2 RCOO^- -> R-R + 2 CO2 at anode, H2 + 2 OH^- at cathode, pH rises!), Soda-lime decarboxylation (RCOONa + NaOH/CaO -> R-H via carbanion stability!).
Halogenation selectivity: Cl2 (1 : 3.8 : 5 for 1 deg : 2 deg : 3 deg H) vs Br2 (1 : 82 : 1600 -> nearly 100% 3 deg substitution!).

Alkene synthesis: E2 dehydrohalogenation (alc. KOH -> Zaitsev more substituted alkene; bulky t-BuOK -> Hofmann less substituted!). Syn-pyrolytic eliminations (ester/xanthate Chugaev/Cope) give Hofmann without carbocation rearrangement!

Electrophilic additions: HBr/H2O+H^+ (Markovnikov via carbocation -> REARRANGES!); Oxymercuration-Demercuration Hg(OAc)2, H2O / NaBH4 (Markovnikov, NO rearrangement!); Hydroboration-Oxidation BH3.THF / H2O2, OH^- (Anti-Markovnikov, STRICT SYN, NO rearrangement!).
Kharasch Peroxide Effect (HBr + ROOR / hv): Free radical chain -> Anti-Markovnikov ONLY with HBr (exothermic propagation; NEVER works with HCl or HI!).

Stereospecific Alkene Additions & Ozonolysis: Br2/CCl4 (Anti via cyclic bromonium: cis-alkene -> racemic; trans-alkene -> meso!); Cold dil. KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent) or OsO4/NaHSO3 (Syn diol: cis -> meso; trans -> racemic!). Reductive ozonolysis (O3 / Zn-H2O or Me2S) gives aldehydes/ketones; Oxidative ozonolysis (O3 / H2O2) or hot KMnO4/H^+ oxidizes =CH- to -COOH and =CH2 to CO2!

sections.heading: Alkynes & Aromatic Hydrocarbons (Benzene EAS & Birch Reduction)
sections.summary: Terminal alkynes possess weakly acidic sp C-H protons (pKa ~25) that form diagnostic metal acetylides, while internal vs terminal alkynes reduce selectively to cis- or trans-alkenes. Benzene undergoes Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) via a resonance-stabilized sigma-complex (arenium ion).
keyPoints: Terminal alkyne tests: R-C#C-H + Na -> R-C#C-Na + 1/2 H2; + Tollen's [Ag(NH3)2]^+ -> white ppt R-C#C-Ag; + Cu2Cl2/NH4OH -> red ppt R-C#C-Cu (differentiates 1-alkynes from 2-alkynes!).

Alkyne reductions & hydration: H2 + Lindlar catalyst (Pd/CaCO3/Pb(OAc)2/quinoline) -> strictly CIS-alkene; Na/liq NH3 (Birch) -> strictly TRANS-alkene! Kucherov hydration (HgSO4 / dil H2SO4): ethyne -> acetaldehyde; terminal alkyne -> methyl ketone; BH3/H2O2 -> terminal aldehyde!
Polymerization & Acidic coupling: 3 CH#CH (red-hot Fe tube, 873 K) -> Benzene; propyne -> Mesitylene (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene).

Benzene EAS Mechanism: Nitration (conc HNO3 + H2SO4 -> NO2^+ electrophile, kinetic isotope effect absent kH = kD!), Sulphonation (conc H2SO4/SO3 -> reversible, kH > kD isotope effect!), Halogenation (X2 + FeX3/AlCl3), Friedel-Crafts Alkylation (carbocation rearranges; polyalkylation occurs; FAILS on strong deactivated rings like nitrobenzene AND on aniline/phenol due to AlCl3 complexation!), FC Acylation (RCOCl/AlCl3 -> NO rearrangement!).
Directing & Activating effects: o/p activators (-NH2, -OH, -OR, -NHCOR, -R); o/p DEACTIVATORS (-F, -Cl, -Br, -I because -I > +M); meta deactivators (-NO2, -CN, -SO3H, -CHO, -COR, -COOH, -NR3^+).

Side-chain oxidation & Birch Reduction: Any alkylbenzene with >=1 benzylic H + hot KMnO4/H^+ -> Benzoic acid (t-Bu-C6H5 fails!); Na/liq NH3/EtOH reduces benzene to 1,4-cyclohexadiene (electron-donating -OMe/-R stays ON the double bond; electron-withdrawing -COOH sits ON the sp3 carbon!).

solvedExamples.question: Arrange the following in decreasing order of acidic strength: (I) Benzoic acid, (II) o-Methylbenzoic acid, (III) p-Methylbenzoic acid, (IV) p-Nitrobenzoic acid, (V) o-Nitrobenzoic acid.
steps: Electron-withdrawing -NO2 (-M, -I) stabilizes carboxylate strongly -> nitrobenzoic acids are much more acidic than benzoic & methylbenzoic acids.
Ortho effect makes BOTH o-nitrobenzoic acid (V) and o-methylbenzoic acid (II) stronger than benzoic acid (I) due to steric inhibition of -COOH resonance and -COO^- solvation.
Between (V) and (IV): o-nitro has both strong -I (closer!) and ortho effect -> (V) > (IV).
Among methyls: (II) o-methyl > (I) benzoic > (III) p-methyl (+I/+H weakens acidity). Overall: (V) > (IV) > (II) > (I) > (III).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Placing o-methylbenzoic acid weaker than benzoic acid by forgetting the steric ortho effect!

solvedExamples.question: 3-Methylbut-1-ene reacts with HBr in the dark (no peroxide) to give major product A, and with HBr in presence of benzoyl peroxide to give major product B. Identify A and B.
steps: Reaction 1 (ionic Markovnikov, no peroxide): H^+ adds to C-1 giving secondary carbocation (CH3)2CH-CH^+-CH3.
1,2-Hydride shift converts the 2 deg carbocation into more stable 3 deg carbocation (CH3)2C^+-CH2-CH3.
Br^- attacks to yield major product A: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
Reaction 2 (HBr + peroxide, radical Anti-Markovnikov): Br radical adds at less hindered C-1 giving 2 deg radical, then H-abstraction yields B: 1-bromo-3-methylbutane (no rearrangement!).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Writing 2-bromo-3-methylbutane for A by missing the 1,2-hydride shift!

solvedExamples.question: An alkene C6H12 on reductive ozonolysis (O3 / Zn-H2O) yields one mole of propanal and one mole of propanone (acetone). Identify the alkene and state how many geometrical isomers it exhibits.
steps: Write structures of products: Propanal = CH3-CH2-CH=O; Propanone = (CH3)2C=O.
Remove both oxygens and fuse the two carbonyl carbons with a C=C double bond: CH3-CH2-CH=C(CH3)2.
IUPAC name: 2-methylpent-2-ene (formula C6H12, DBE = 1).
Check C=C substituents: C-2 carries two identical -CH3 groups => CANNOT show geometrical isomerism (0 geometrical isomers)!
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming every alkene formed from two different carbonyls shows cis/trans isomerism!

solvedExamples.question: Starting from Benzene, design the sequence to synthesize m-nitrochlorobenzene vs p-nitrochlorobenzene selectively, and explain why cis-but-2-ene + Br2/CCl4 gives an optically inactive mixture.
steps: For p-nitrochlorobenzene: (1) Chlorinate first (Cl2/FeCl3 -> chlorobenzene; -Cl is o/p directing), (2) Nitrate (HNO3/H2SO4 -> major para-nitrochlorobenzene + minor ortho).
For m-nitrochlorobenzene: REVERSE the order! (1) Nitrate first (HNO3/H2SO4 -> nitrobenzene; -NO2 is strong meta director), (2) Chlorinate (Cl2/FeCl3 -> m-nitrochlorobenzene).
For cis-but-2-ene + Br2/CCl4: Br2 forms a symmetric cyclic bromonium ion; Br^- opens it via ANTI backside attack equally at C-2 and C-3.
This stereospecific anti-addition on cis-but-2-ene generates an exact 50:50 racemic mixture of (2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane -> optically inactive by external compensation!
solvedExamples.answer: Para = Cl2/FeCl3 then HNO3/H2SO4; Meta = HNO3/H2SO4 then Cl2/FeCl3; cis + Br2 -> racemic (optically inactive)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using trans-but-2-ene + Br2 gives Meso (internally inactive), whereas cis-but-2-ene gives Racemic (externally inactive)!
