sections.heading: Haloalkanes & Haloarenes: SN1, SN2, E1, E2, NGP & ArSN
sections.summary: Nucleophilic substitution and elimination compete directly depending on substrate degree, nucleophile basicity, leaving group ability (I^- > Br^- > Cl^- > F^-), and solvent polarity. Neighboring Group Participation (NGP) accelerates solvolysis dramatically with double inversion giving net retention.
keyPoints: SN2 (bimolecular, 1-step, Walden inversion): Rate = k[R-X][Nu^-]; order CH3X > 1 deg > 2 deg >> 3 deg (neopentyl halide fails due to steric block!); favored by POLAR APROTIC solvents (DMSO, DMF, acetone) and strong unhindered nucleophiles.

SN1 (unimolecular, 2-step, racemization + partial inversion + carbocation rearrangement): Rate = k[R-X]; order Ph3CX > Benzyl ~ Allyl ~ 3 deg > 2 deg >> 1 deg; favored by POLAR PROTIC solvents (H2O, EtOH, HCOOH) and Ag^+ catalysis!

E2 vs E1: E2 requires strict ANTI-PERIPLANAR H and X (trans-diaxial in cyclohexane!), shows deuterium isotope effect (k_H/k_D ~ 6), gives Zaitsev alkene with EtO^- and Hofmann (less substituted) with bulky t-BuOK! E1 occurs via carbocation with rearrangement.

NGP (Anchimeric Assistance): Beta-halo sulfides (mustard gas type), beta-acetoxy or phenyl-bridged phenonium systems react orders of magnitude faster via cyclic intermediate -> 2 successive SN2 inversions yield 100% RETENTION of configuration!

Halide syntheses & named reactions: Finkelstein (R-Cl/Br + NaI/acetone -> R-I + NaCl ppt), Swarts (R-Cl + AgF/SbF3/Hg2F2 -> R-F), Darzens (ROH + SOCl2/Pyridine -> inverted R-Cl; without pyridine SNi -> retained R-Cl!).

Haloarenes: Inert to normal SN1/SN2 (partial C=X double bond + sp2 C + unstable Ph^+). Undergoes Dow's process (PhCl + NaOH, 623 K, 300 atm -> phenol via benzyne!) or ArSN addition-elimination easily when o/p -NO2 groups stabilize Meisenheimer carbanion (2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene hydrolyzes in warm water!).

sections.heading: Alcohols, Phenols & Ethers: Oxidations, Rearrangements & Ether Cleavage
sections.summary: Alcohol reactivity splits between O-H cleavage (acidity: CH3OH > 1 deg > 2 deg > 3 deg) and C-O cleavage (Lucas/dehydration: 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg). Phenols undergo facile ortho/para electrophilic attack, whereas unsymmetrical ethers cleave with HI via SN2 or SN1 depending on alkyl branching.
keyPoints: Alcohol distinguishing tests: Lucas (conc HCl + anhy ZnCl2): 3 deg immediate cloudiness, 2 deg in 5 min, 1 deg no room-T turbidity (allylic/benzylic also fast!). Victor Meyer (P/I2 -> AgNO2 -> HNO2 -> KOH): 1 deg Blood Red, 2 deg Blue, 3 deg Colourless!

Selective Oxidations: PCC / Collin's / PDC oxidize 1 deg ROH -> RCHO (stops cleanly at aldehyde!), 2 deg -> ketone; Jones (CrO3/H2SO4) or KMnO4 oxidizes 1 deg -> RCOOH; MnO2 selectively oxidizes ONLY allylic/benzylic alcohols; Hot Cu/573 K: 1 deg -> aldehyde, 2 deg -> ketone, 3 deg -> ALKENE (dehydration!).
Pinacol-Pinacolone Rearrangement: Vicinal diol + H^+ -> carbocation -> 1,2-migration (migratory aptitude: H > Ph/aryl > 3 deg > 2 deg > Me) -> ketone!

Phenol classics: Reimer-Tiemann (Phenol + CHCl3 + aq KOH -> Salicylaldehyde via :CCl2 carbene; with CCl4/KOH -> Salicylic acid); Kolbe-Schmidt (PhONa + CO2, 400 K, 4-7 atm -> Salicylic acid); Fries rearrangement (phenyl acetate + AlCl3 -> o/p-hydroxyacetophenone); Br2/H2O -> 2,4,6-tribromophenol white ppt vs Br2/CS2 -> p-bromophenol; Neutral FeCl3 -> violet colour!
Williamson Ether Synthesis (R-ONa + R'-X -> R-O-R'): R'-X MUST be 1 deg (or CH3) halide! Using 3 deg halide (t-BuBr + EtO^-) gives E2 isobutene instead of ether!

HI Ether Cleavage: Cold conc HI cleaves 1 deg/2 deg alkyl ethers by SN2 at the LESS hindered carbon (Me-O-Et -> MeI + EtOH); BUT if one group forms a stable carbocation (tert-butyl, benzyl, allyl), SN1 occurs (t-Bu-O-Me + HI -> t-BuI + MeOH)! Anisole (Ph-O-Me) + HI ALWAYS gives Phenol + CH3I (sp2 C-O never breaks!).

sections.heading: Aldehydes & Ketones: Nucleophilic Addition, Aldol, Cannizzaro & Haloform
sections.summary: Polar carbonyl C=O carbons undergo nucleophilic addition faster in aldehydes than ketones (HCHO > RCHO > ArCHO > R2CO > Ar2CO) due to lower steric hindrance and weaker +I/+M stabilization. Alpha-hydrogens render aldehydes/ketones weakly acidic (pKa ~17-20), driving enolate Aldol condensations while alpha-H-less aldehydes undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation.
keyPoints: Nucleophilic additions & tests: HCN (cyanohydrin), NaHSO3 (white crystalline adduct for purification, fails hindered ketones like PhCOPh), ROH/dry HCl (hemiacetal -> acetal, stable in base!), NH2-OH (oxime), 2,4-DNP Brady's test (orange-red hydrazone for ALL aldehydes & ketones).

Reductions: LiAlH4 / NaBH4 -> alcohols; Clemmensen (Zn-Hg / conc HCl -> C=O to CH2, acid-sensitive groups fail!); Wolff-Kishner (NH2NH2 / KOH, ethylene glycol -> C=O to CH2, base-sensitive halides/esters fail!); Red P + HI -> alkane; MPV reduction (Al(OiPr)3) & Oppenauer oxidation.

Oxidations: Tollens' [Ag(NH3)2]^+ (silver mirror for ALL aldehydes incl. PhCHO & HCOOH!); Fehling's (Cu^2+ tartrate brick-red Cu2O) & Benedict's reduce aliphatic aldehydes ONLY (FAIL for benzaldehyde!); Baeyer-Villiger (RCO3H -> ester/lactone; migratory aptitude H > 3 deg > cyclohexyl > 2 deg ~ Ph > 1 deg > Me!).

Aldol Condensation (dil. NaOH, requires >=1 alpha-H): forms beta-hydroxy aldehyde/ketone -> on heating eliminates H2O to alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl (Cross-aldol gives 4 products unless one partner lacks alpha-H like PhCHO/HCHO!). Intramolecular aldol preferentially forms stable 5- or 6-membered rings!

Cannizzaro Reaction (conc. 50% NaOH, ZERO alpha-H: HCHO, PhCHO, Me3CCHO, CCl3CHO): disproportionates to 1 alcohol + 1 carboxylate salt. In Crossed-Cannizzaro with HCHO, HCHO ALWAYS oxidizes to HCOO^- while the other aldehyde reduces to RCH2OH! Intramolecular Cannizzaro (glyoxal -> glycolate).

Haloform Reaction (X2 + NaOH or NaOX): Positive yellow CHI3 ppt for CH3-C(=O)-R (acetaldehyde, methyl ketones) AND CH3-CH(OH)-R (ethanol, 2-propanol, 2-butanol). Note: CH3OH & carboxylic acids/esters/amides (CH3COCl, CH3COOH, CH3COOEt) FAIL haloform!

sections.heading: Carboxylic Acids & Acid Derivatives (Acyl Nucleophilic Substitution)
sections.summary: Carboxylic acids dimeric H-bonding elevates boiling points above alcohols, while resonance-stabilized carboxylate anions make them far more acidic than phenols. Acid derivatives interconvert via tetrahedral addition-elimination at rates mirroring leaving-group ability (RCOCl > (RCO)2O > RCOOR' > RCONH2).
keyPoints: Carboxylic Acidity: FCH2COOH > ClCH2COOH > BrCH2COOH > ICH2COOH > HCOOH > PhCOOH > CH3COOH > RCH2COOH (dicarboxylic acids: Oxalic pKa1 1.25 > Malonic > Succinic; maleic cis pKa1 << fumaric trans due to maleate intramolecular H-bond, while pKa2 reverses!).
Acid Synthesis: Primary alcohol/aldehyde + KMnO4/Jones; Alkylbenzene + KMnO4; Nitrile hydrolysis (R-CN + H3O^+); Grignard + dry ice CO2/H3O^+ (adds 1 carbon!).
HVZ (Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky) Reaction: R-CH2-COOH + X2 (Cl2 or Br2) / Red P -> alpha-halo carboxylic acid R-CH(X)-COOH (requires at least one alpha-H; HCOOH fails!).

Decarboxylation: Beta-keto acids (R-CO-CH2-COOH) and gem-dicarboxylic acids (malonic acid) decarboxylate effortlessly on gentle warming via cyclic 6-membered TS! Sodium salts + Soda-lime (NaOH/CaO, heat) give alkanes.

Derivative Reductions: Rosenmund (RCOCl + H2 / Pd-BaSO4 -> RCHO); Stephen (RCN + SnCl2/HCl then H3O^+ -> RCHO); DIBAL-H at -78 C (RCN or RCOOR' -> RCHO cleanly!); Bouveault-Blanc (ester + Na/EtOH -> alcohols); LiAlH4 reduces ALL derivatives (-COOH, -COCl, -COOR -> 1 deg ROH; -CONH2 -> RCH2NH2!).

Amide-to-Amine Rearrangements (100% chiral retention!): Hoffmann Bromamide (RCONH2 + Br2 + 4 KOH -> R-NH2 + K2CO3, 1 carbon LESS); Curtius (RCON3 + heat -> RN=C=O -> RNH2); Schmidt (RCOOH + HN3/H2SO4 -> RNH2).

sections.heading: Amines & Diazonium Salts: Basicity Orders, Hinsberg, Gabriel & Coupling
sections.summary: Amine basicity in the gas phase strictly tracks +I alkyl donation (3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg > NH3), whereas aqueous basicity balances +I stabilization against cation hydration and steric hindrance. Aromatic diazonium salts (ArN2^+ Cl^- stable at 0-5 C) serve as the master synthetic hub for introducing -F, -Cl, -Br, -I, -CN, -OH, -H, and azo dyes.
keyPoints: Basicity in Water: Methylamines (CH3)2NH (2 deg) > CH3NH2 (1 deg) > (CH3)3N (3 deg) > NH3; Ethylamines (C2H5)2NH (2 deg) > (C2H5)3N (3 deg) > C2H5NH2 (1 deg) > NH3! In chlorobenzene/gas phase: 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg > NH3.

Aryl vs Aliphatic: Cyclohexylamine >> Aniline (sp2 lone pair delocalized into ring!). Para-methoxyaniline > p-toluidine > aniline > m-nitroaniline > p-nitroaniline > o-nitroaniline (ortho + SIR + H-bond!).

Pure 1 deg Amine Syntheses: Gabriel Phthalimide (Phthalimide + KOH + R-X -> R-NH2; works ONLY for 1 deg aliphatic halides, NEVER Ar-X or 3 deg R-X!); Hoffmann Bromamide (step-down); Mendius (RCN + Na/EtOH or LiAlH4 -> RCH2NH2).

Diagnostic Amine Tests: Carbylamine (CHCl3 + alc KOH -> foul R-NC isocyanide, ONLY 1 deg aliphatic & aromatic amines!); Hinsberg (PhSO2Cl: 1 deg forms PhSO2NHR soluble in KOH; 2 deg forms PhSO2NR2 insoluble in KOH; 3 deg does NOT react!); Nitrosation (NaNO2 + HCl: 1 deg aliphatic -> N2 gas + ROH/alkene; 2 deg -> yellow oily N-nitrosamine -> Liebermann test; 3 deg aliphatic -> soluble salt; N,N-dimethylaniline -> green p-nitroso!).

Aniline EAS traps: Direct nitration (HNO3/H2SO4) gives 47% meta! Direct bromination (Br2/H2O) gives white 2,4,6-tribromoaniline! To get clean para-bromo/nitroaniline, PROTECT -NH2 as acetanilide (-NHCOCH3) using Ac2O/Py first, run EAS, then hydrolyze!

Diazonium Reactions (Ar-NH2 + NaNO2/HCl at 0-5 C -> Ar-N2^+ Cl^-): CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr or CuCN (Sandmeyer); Cu/HCl (Gattermann); KI (Ar-I); HBF4/heat (Balz-Schiemann Ar-F); H3PO2/H2O or EtOH (Ar-H); H2O/283+ K (Phenol); Coupling with Phenol (weak base pH 9-10 -> p-hydroxyazobenzene ORANGE dye) or Aniline (weak acid pH 4-5 -> p-aminoazobenzene YELLOW dye).

sections.heading: Chemoselectivity & Multi-Step Organic Conversion Roadmaps
sections.summary: Solving multi-reagent synthetic cascades requires tracking carbon count changes (step-up via Grignard/CN^-/Aldol vs step-down via Hoffmann/Haloform/Decarboxylation/Ozonolysis) alongside reagent chemoselectivity. NaBH4 spares esters/acids/nitro/alkenes, whereas LiAlH4 reduces almost all polar carbonyls while sparing isolated C=C bonds.
keyPoints: Hydride Chemoselectivity: NaBH4 reduces ONLY RCOCl, RCHO, RCOR' (spares -COOH, -COOR, -CONH2, -CN, -NO2, C=C); LiAlH4 reduces ALL carbonyls, acids, esters, nitriles, epoxides, nitro (to azo in ArNO2!) while sparing isolated C=C (Exception: cinnamaldehyde Ph-CH=CH-CHO -> Ph-CH=CH-CH2OH with NaBH4, Ph-CH2-CH2-CH2OH with LiAlH4!).
Diborane (B2H6/THF): Reduces -COOH -> -CH2OH FASTEST (faster than esters/ketones/nitro!).
Carbon Step-Up tools (+1 C): R-X + KCN -> RCN -> RCOOH / RCH2NH2; R-MgX + HCHO -> RCH2OH; R-MgX + CO2 -> RCOOH; Arndt-Eistert.
Carbon Step-Down tools (-1 C): Hoffmann Bromamide (RCONH2 -> RNH2); Haloform (RCOCH3 -> RCOOH); Soda-lime decarboxylation (RCOONa -> R-H); Ozonolysis.

Distinguishing pairs: Formic vs Acetic acid (HCOOH reduces Tollens' & decolorizes KMnO4!); Benzaldehyde vs Acetaldehyde (CH3CHO gives Fehling's & Iodoform; PhCHO fails both!); Phenol vs Benzoic acid (PhCOOH gives CO2 with NaHCO3; Phenol gives violet FeCl3!).

solvedExamples.question: Identify major products when tert-butyl methyl ether ((CH3)3C-O-CH3) is treated with (a) 1 eq cold HI and (b) excess hot HI; contrast with ethyl methyl ether + 1 eq cold HI.
steps: Protonation of (CH3)3C-O-CH3 gives oxonium ion (CH3)3C-O^+(H)-CH3.
Because (CH3)3C^+ is a highly stable tertiary carbocation, C-O cleavage follows SN1 pathway -> gives (CH3)3C-I + CH3OH with 1 eq cold HI! Excess hot HI turns CH3OH into CH3I as well.
In contrast, ethyl methyl ether (CH3CH2-O-CH3) cannot form a stable 1 deg carbocation -> follows SN2 attack by I^- at the less sterically hindered methyl carbon.
Result for ethyl methyl ether + 1 eq cold HI: CH3I + CH3CH2OH.
solvedExamples.answer: t-BuOMe + cold HI -> t-BuI + MeOH; EtOMe + cold HI -> MeI + EtOH
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying SN2 (MeI + t-BuOH) to tert-butyl methyl ether ignores SN1 carbocation stability!

solvedExamples.question: Predict the major product when (A) Benzaldehyde + Formaldehyde react with 50% NaOH, and (B) 2-Methylpropanal reacts with 50% NaOH vs dil. NaOH.
steps: (A) Both PhCHO and HCHO lack alpha-H => Crossed-Cannizzaro occurs. Formaldehyde is sterically less hindered and hydrates/transfers hydride faster -> HCHO oxidizes to HCOONa while PhCHO reduces to Benzyl alcohol (PhCH2OH).

(B) 2-Methylpropanal ((CH3)2CH-CHO) HAS one alpha-H! With dil. NaOH it undergoes Aldol condensation (gives 3-hydroxy-2,2,4-trimethylpentanal, which CANNOT dehydrate easily because C-2 has no remaining alpha-H!).
With conc. 50% NaOH (and heat), 2-methylpropanal is a famous exception that can undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation in competing conditions, OR primarily aldol addition first.
Key takeaway: always check alpha-H count AND base concentration!
solvedExamples.pitfall: Oxidizing PhCHO to PhCOONa in Crossed-Cannizzaro with HCHO!

solvedExamples.question: Arrange the following in decreasing order of pKb (increasing order of basic strength) in aqueous solution: C2H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, (C2H5)3N, NH3, C6H5NH2.
steps: Recall pKb = -log10(Kb): LOWER pKb means STRONGER base.
Aniline (C6H5NH2) has lone pair delocalized into benzene ring -> weakest base (highest pKb).
Among aliphatic ethylamines in water, solvation + +I + sterics give basicity order: 2 deg > 3 deg > 1 deg > NH3.
Thus basicity increases as: C6H5NH2 < NH3 < C2H5NH2 < (C2H5)3N < (C2H5)2NH (decreasing pKb order is exact same!).
solvedExamples.answer: Decreasing pKb (Increasing basicity): C6H5NH2 > NH3 > C2H5NH2 > (C2H5)3N > (C2H5)2NH
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing Methylamine aqueous order (2 > 1 > 3) with Ethylamine aqueous order (2 > 3 > 1)!

solvedExamples.question: An optically active compound A (C8H10O) gives a yellow precipitate with I2/NaOH, turns CrO3/H2SO4 orange-green, and on vigorous oxidation with hot KMnO4 yields benzoic acid. Treating A with PBr3 gives inverted B, which on reaction with aq. KOH/acetone yields inverted C? Wait: let's track stereochemistry! Treating (R)-1-phenylethanol (A) with SOCl2 in pyridine gives B, and with TsCl/pyridine followed by CH3COO^- gives C. Determine R/S configuration of B and C.
steps: Check A: (R)-1-phenylethanol (Ph-CH(OH)-CH3) has methyl-carbinol group -> positive Iodoform test, oxidized by CrO3, oxidized by hot KMnO4 to PhCOOH.
Step 1 (SOCl2 + Pyridine = Darzens): Pyridine attacks HCl and drives backside SN2 displacement of chlorosulfite leaving group => 100% INVERSION -> B is (S)-1-chloro-1-phenylethane.
Step 2 (TsCl/Py): Converts -OH into -OTs WITHOUT breaking the chiral C-O bond => retention of (R) configuration!
Step 3 (+ CH3COO^-): Acetate displaces -OTs via backside SN2 => INVERSION -> C is (S)-1-phenylethyl acetate!
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming SOCl2 without pyridine (SNi retention) and SOCl2 + pyridine (SN2 inversion) give the same stereoisomer!

sections.heading: Carbohydrates: Glucose Structure Proofs, Anomers, Mutarotation & Disaccharides
sections.summary: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones (all monosaccharides and reducing disaccharides reduce Tollens'/Fehling's via free hemiacetal/hemiketal rings). Sucrose locks both anomeric carbons (alpha-C1 of glucose to beta-C2 of fructose), making it non-reducing and devoid of mutarotation.
keyPoints: Glucose open-chain proofs: + HI/Red P -> n-hexane (6-C linear); + NH2OH/HCN -> oxime/cyanohydrin (1 C=O); + Br2/H2O -> Gluconic acid (aldehyde group); + conc HNO3 -> Saccharic acid (1 deg -OH + -CHO); + 5 Ac2O -> pentaacetate (5 -OH).

Cyclic hemiacetal proofs (Pyranose ring): Glucose FAILS Schiff's test & NaHSO3 adduct! Pentaacetate FAILS NH2OH (no free C1-OH!). Forms two crystalline anomers (C1 epimers): alpha-D-(+)-glucopyranose (+112 deg, 36%) and beta-D-(+)-glucopyranose (+19 deg, 64%) -> equilibrate in water to +52.5 deg (MUTAROTATION!).
Osazone identity: Glucose, Mannose (C2 epimer!), and Fructose (ketose!) react with 3 eq PhNHNH2 to form the EXACT SAME yellow crystalline glucosazone needles (C1 & C2 stereocentres destroyed!).
Fructose reduces Tollens'/Fehling's via Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein enediol tautomerization in basic medium into glucose/mannose!

Disaccharides: Sucrose (alpha-D-Glc C1 <-> beta-D-Fru C2; non-reducing, no mutarotation; invert sugar flips +66.5 deg -> +52.5 - 92.4 = -39.9 deg net levo!); Maltose (alpha-D-Glc C1->C4, reducing); Lactose (beta-D-Gal C1->C4 beta-D-Glc, reducing).

Polysaccharides: Starch = Amylose (15-20%, water-soluble, unbranched alpha-1,4, blue with I2) + Amylopectin (80-85%, insoluble, branched alpha-1,4 & alpha-1,6); Glycogen (animal starch, more branched); Cellulose (unbranched beta-1,4-D-glucose, most abundant organic biomolecule!).

sections.heading: Amino Acids, Zwitterions (pI), Proteins & Enzymes
sections.summary: Natural alpha-amino acids carry L-configuration (except optically inactive Glycine) and exist predominantly as dipolar zwitterions at neutral pH. Peptide amide bonds (-CO-NH-) link amino acids into primary sequences folded via H-bonding and disulphide bridges into fibrous or globular proteins.
keyPoints: 20 amino acids: Only Glycine is achiral! Essential (10, mnemonic PVT TIM HALL: Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg, Leu, Lys); Acidic (Asp, Glu); Basic (Lys, Arg, His); Sulphur-containing (Cys forms -S-S- disulphide, Met).

Zwitterion & Isoelectric Point (pI): At pH < pI -> cationic (migrates to cathode); at pH > pI -> anionic (migrates to anode); at pH = pI -> zero net mobility & minimum solubility! Neutral AA: pI = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2; Acidic AA (Asp/Glu): average TWO LOWEST pKa values; Basic AA (Lys/Arg): average TWO HIGHEST pKa values.

Peptide test: Biuret test (alkaline CuSO4 -> violet colour for >= 2 peptide bonds, i.e. tripeptides and proteins; dipeptides fail!). Ninhydrin test -> Ruhemann's purple for amino acids (Proline gives yellow!).

Protein Structures: Primary (covalent peptide sequence), Secondary (alpha-helix intramolecular H-bond & beta-pleated sheet intermolecular H-bond), Tertiary (H-bond, disulphide, ionic, hydrophobic folding), Quaternary (multi-subunit haemoglobin).

Fibrous vs Globular: Fibrous (water-insoluble, Keratin, Myosin, Collagen) vs Globular (water-soluble, Insulin, Albumin, Haemoglobin, Enzymes). Denaturation (heat/pH/urea) destroys 2 deg, 3 deg & 4 deg structures while leaving 1 deg peptide sequence intact!
Enzymes: Specific protein biocatalysts lowering E_a; Invertase (sucrose -> Glc+Fru), Zymase (Glc -> EtOH), Urease, Maltase.

sections.heading: Vitamins, Hormones & Nucleic Acids (DNA & RNA)
sections.summary: Vitamins are essential organic micronutrients classified into liver-stored fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and regularly excreted water-soluble (B-complex, C) groups. Nucleic acids are polynucleotides linked by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds pairing complementary purines and pyrimidines via specific hydrogen bonds.
keyPoints: Fat-soluble Vitamins: A (Retinol -> Xerophthalmia / Night blindness), D (Calciferol -> Rickets / Osteomalacia), E (Tocopherol -> RBC fragility / sterility), K (Phylloquinone -> delayed blood clotting).

Water-soluble Vitamins: B1 (Thiamine -> Beri-Beri), B2 (Riboflavin -> Cheilosis), B6 (Pyridoxine -> Convulsions), B12 (Cyanocobalamin, contains Cobalt! -> Pernicious anaemia), C (Ascorbic acid -> Scurvy, bleeding gums).
Nucleic Acid Sugars & Bases: DNA = beta-D-2-deoxyribose + Purines (Adenine, Guanine) + Pyrimidines (Cytosine, Thymine); RNA = beta-D-ribose + A, G, C, Uracil (NO Thymine!).
Nucleoside (Sugar + Base at C1') vs Nucleotide (Sugar + Base + Phosphate at C5'). Polymerizes via 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage.
DNA Double Helix & Chargaff's Rule: Antiparallel strands; A = T (2 H-bonds), G === C (3 H-bonds, higher GC % raises DNA melting temperature T_m!).
Hormones: Steroid (cortisol, testosterone, estradiol), Polypeptide (insulin lowers blood sugar, glucagon raises), Amino-acid derivatives (thyroxine, epinephrine).

sections.heading: Qualitative Inorganic Analysis I: Dry Tests & Anion Identification
sections.summary: Preliminary flame and borax-bead tests provide rapid cation clues, followed by systematic acid treatment separating anions into dilute-H2SO4 volatile, concentrated-H2SO4 volatile, and independent sulphate/phosphate groups. Specific confirmatory complexes eliminate interfering ions.

sections.summary: Cation separation exploits systematic pH and common-ion tuning of H2S and NH4OH so sulphides and hydroxides precipitate strictly in order of K_sp. Practical organic analysis pairs Lassaigne sodium-fusion hetero-atom tests with quantitative redox titrations.

HCl + H2S -> low-Ksp sulphides): IIA (insoluble in yellow (NH4)2S_x): HgS (black, soluble ONLY in aqua regia), PbS (black), Bi2S3 (brown/black), CuS (black -> dissolves in dil HNO3, excess NH4OH deep blue [Cu(NH3)4]^2+, + K4[Fe(CN)6] chocolate brown Cu2[Fe(CN)6]!), CdS (canary yellow); IIB (soluble in yellow (NH4)2S_x): As2S3 (yellow), Sb2S3 (orange), SnS (brown)/SnS2 (yellow).

solvedExamples.question: Calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of Glutamic acid (pKa1 = 2.19, pKaR = 4.25, pKa2 = 9.67) and Lysine (pKa1 = 2.18, pKa2 = 8.95, pKaR = 10.53), and determine the net charge of Glutamic acid at pH 7.0.
steps: For acidic amino acid (Glutamic acid, extra -COOH in side chain), zwitterion sits between the two acidic dissociations: pI = (pKa1 + pKaR) / 2 = (2.19 + 4.25) / 2 = 3.22.
For basic amino acid (Lysine, extra -NH2 in side chain), zwitterion sits between the two basic dissociations: pI = (pKa2 + pKaR) / 2 = (8.95 + 10.53) / 2 = 9.74.
At pH 7.0 (> pI = 3.22 and > pKaR = 4.25, < pKa2 = 9.67), both alpha-COOH and side-chain -COOH are deprotonated (-1 each) while -NH3^+ stays protonated (+1).
Net charge on Glutamic acid at pH 7.0 = -1 - 1 + 1 = -1 (migrates toward ANODE!).
solvedExamples.answer: pI(Glu) = 3.22, pI(Lys) = 9.74; Glu net charge at pH 7 = -1 (anode)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Averaging all three pKa values or averaging pKa1 and pKa2 for acidic/basic amino acids!

solvedExamples.question: During Lassaigne's test for an organic compound containing BOTH Nitrogen and Sulphur (like thiourea), what happens if insufficient Sodium vs excess Sodium is fused, and what colours appear with FeCl3 vs sodium nitroprusside?
steps: With insufficient Sodium, N and S fuse together to form Sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN).
Adding FeCl3 to NaSCN produces a BLOOD-RED colouration due to [Fe(SCN)(H2O)5]^2+ (neither Prussian blue nor nitroprusside violet appears!).
With EXCESS Sodium, NaSCN splits completely: NaSCN + 2 Na -> NaCN + Na2S.
Then FeSO4/FeCl3 yields Prussian blue Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (for N) and sodium nitroprusside gives violet [Fe(CN)5(NOS)]^4- (for S) independently!
solvedExamples.answer: Insufficient Na -> NaSCN -> blood-red with FeCl3; Excess Na -> NaCN + Na2S -> separate Prussian blue & violet tests
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing the blood-red [Fe(SCN)]^2+ complex of N+S with the Brown Ring [Fe(H2O)5(NO)]^2+ test for nitrate!

solvedExamples.question: Which of the following carbohydrates will NOT exhibit mutarotation and will NOT reduce Tollens' reagent, and why? (A) Maltose, (B) Lactose, (C) Sucrose, (D) Fructose.
steps: Mutarotation and Tollens' reduction require a FREE hemiacetal or hemiketal -OH group at the anomeric carbon capable of opening into a carbonyl.
Maltose (alpha-1,4) and Lactose (beta-1,4) still retain a free anomeric C1-OH on the second glucose ring -> reducing + mutarotation.
Fructose has a free C2 hemiketal -> undergoes base-catalyzed enediol tautomerization -> reducing + mutarotation.
Sucrose links C1 of alpha-D-glucose directly to C2 of beta-D-fructose as a locked acetal-ketal glycoside -> ZERO free anomeric -OH -> non-reducing, NO mutarotation!
solvedExamples.pitfall: Thinking Fructose is non-reducing because it is a ketohexose!

solvedExamples.question: An inorganic salt mixture dissolved in water gives NO ppt with dil. HCl, a black ppt (A) with H2S in dil. HCl that dissolves in 50% HNO3 giving blue solution (B). Adding excess NH4OH to (B) yields deep blue (C), while NH4Cl + NH4OH on the original filtrate gives a dirty green ppt (D) that turns yellow solution (E) with NaOH + H2O2. Identify A, B, C, D, E.
steps: No ppt with dil. HCl rules out Group I (Ag^+, Pb^2+, Hg2^2+). Black ppt (A) with HCl + H2S dissolving in 50% HNO3 to blue solution (B) identifies Cu^2+: A = CuS, B = Cu(NO3)2.
Excess NH4OH on Cu^2+ forms tetraamminecopper(II) deep blue complex C = [Cu(NH3)4]^2+.
Group III (NH4Cl + NH4OH) dirty green ppt is Chromium(III) hydroxide: D = Cr(OH)3.
Alkaline H2O2 oxidizes Cr(OH)3 (+3) to yellow chromate solution: E = Na2CrO4 (CrO4^2-).
solvedExamples.answer: A = CuS, B = Cu(NO3)2, C = [Cu(NH3)4]^2+, D = Cr(OH)3, E = Na2CrO4
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing Ni^2+/Co^2+ (Group IV sulphides) with CuS (Group II sulphide), or Fe(OH)3 (red-brown) with Cr(OH)3 (green)!

sections.heading: Ideal Gas Mixtures, Graham's Effusion & Eudiometry Extensions
sections.summary: Gas pressure arises from elastic molecular wall collisions and obeys Dalton's law of partial pressures (P_i = X_i P_total) for non-reacting mixtures. Effusion rates scale inversely with sqrt(M) and directly with partial pressure, enabling isotopic enrichment calculations.
keyPoints: Gas Laws: Boyle (PV = const at const T,n), Charles (V/T = const at const P,n), Gay-Lussac (P/T = const), Avogadro (V/n = const). Combined PV = nRT -> density d = PM / (RT).
Dalton's Law & Aqueous Tension: P_total = P_1 + P_2 + ...; P_dry_gas = P_moist_gas - P_water_vapour (aqueous tension depends ONLY on temperature!).
Connected Bulb Problems: Conserve total moles n1 + n2 = n1' + n2' => P_1 V_1 / T_1 + P_2 V_2 / T_2 = P_f (V_1/T_1' + V_2/T_2').

Graham's Law of Effusion/Diffusion: Rate r = (dn/dt) proportional to (P * A) / sqrt(M * T). At equal T, P: r1 / r2 = sqrt(M2 / M1). For multi-step effusion enrichment: (n_A / n_B)_after_k_steps = (n_A / n_B)_initial * (M_B / M_A)^(k/2).
Barometric & Manometric traps: Tilted tube height h_vertical = L sin(theta); capillary air-trapped barometer P_atm = P_Hg + P_air.

sections.heading: Kinetic Theory of Gases (KTG) & Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
sections.summary: KTG models ideal gases as point particles with zero intermolecular forces whose average translational kinetic energy depends solely on absolute temperature (3/2 k_B T per molecule). The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution predicts characteristic speeds (u_mp < u_avg < u_rms) and collision frequencies.
keyPoints: KTG Pressure Equation: P V = (1/3) m N u_rms^2 = (2/3) KE_trans => Translational KE = (3/2) n R T (independent of gas molar mass or atomicity!).
Three Speeds: u_mp = sqrt(2RT/M), u_avg = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)), u_rms = sqrt(3RT/M). Ratio u_mp : u_avg : u_rms = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224 = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3).

Maxwell-Boltzmann Curve (fraction dN/N vs speed u): Area under curve = 1 (constant!). Raising T shifts peak right (higher u_mp) and lowers peak height (curve flattens); He (lighter) has wider, flatter curve than N2 (heavier) at same T!
Collision parameters: Mean free path lambda = 1 / [sqrt(2) pi d^2 (N/V)] = (k_B T) / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 P) (at constant V, lambda is independent of T; at constant P, lambda proportional to T!).
Collision frequency: Z_1 (single molecule) = sqrt(2) pi d^2 u_avg (N/V); Z_11 (total bimolecular collisions/vol/s) = (1/sqrt(2)) pi d^2 u_avg (N/V)^2.

sections.heading: Real Gases: Van der Waals Equation, Virial Form & Critical Constants
sections.summary: Real gases deviate from ideality due to intermolecular attraction 'a' (reducing wall pressure by a n^2/V^2) and finite molecular co-volume 'b' (reducing free volume by nb). Compressibility factor Z = PV_m / (RT) directly maps attraction-dominated (Z < 1) vs repulsion-dominated (Z > 1) pressure regimes.
keyPoints: Van der Waals Equation: (P + a n^2 / V^2)(V - n b) = n R T. Units: a -> atm L^2 mol^(-2); b -> L mol^(-1). Excluded co-volume b = 4 * N_A * (4/3 pi r^3) = 4 x actual molar molecular volume!
Meaning of a & b: Higher 'a' means stronger attraction and EASIER liquefaction (NH3, SO2, CO2 >> H2, He); higher 'b' means larger molecular size.

Compressibility Regimes (Z vs P): Very low P -> Z -> 1; Moderate P -> Z = 1 - a/(V_m RT) < 1 (attraction wins, easier compression); High P -> Z = 1 + Pb/(RT) > 1 (repulsion wins). Exception: H2 & He have tiny 'a', so Z > 1 at ALL pressures at 298 K!

Virial Expansion & Boyle Temperature: Z = 1 + B(T)/V_m + C(T)/V_m^2 + ..., where second virial coefficient B(T) = b - a/(R T). At Boyle Temperature T_B = a / (R b), B(T_B) = 0 so gas behaves nearly ideal over a wide low-to-moderate pressure range!

Critical Constants (inflection point of P-V isotherm): V_c = 3 b, P_c = a / (27 b^2), T_c = 8a / (27 R b). Universal Critical Compressibility Z_c = P_c V_c / (R T_c) = 3/8 = 0.375! Ratios: T_B = (27/8) T_c; Inversion Temp (Joule-Thomson) T_i = 2a / (R b) = 2 T_B (cooling occurs ONLY when T < T_i!).

sections.heading: Solid State: 7 Crystal Systems, Cubic Unit Cells & Packing Efficiency
sections.summary: Crystalline solids exhibit sharp melting points and anisotropy due to long-range periodic order across 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices. Unit cell edge-radius geometry determines effective atom count Z, coordination number, packing fraction, and crystal density rho = (Z * M) / (N_A * a^3).
keyPoints: 7 Crystal Systems (CTOMRHT): Cubic (a=b=c, 90/90/90), Tetragonal (a=b!=c, 90), Orthorhombic (a!=b!=c, 90 -> 4 Bravais types!), Monoclinic (a!=b!=c, alpha=gamma=90!=beta), Rhombohedral (a=b=c, alpha=beta=gamma!=90), Hexagonal (a=b!=c, 90/90/120), Triclinic (most unsymmetrical: a!=b!=c, alpha!=beta!=gamma!=90).
Cubic Unit Cells: SC (Z=1, a=2r, CN=6, PE=52.4%); BCC (Z=2, sqrt(3)a=4r, CN=8, PE=68.0%); FCC/CCP (Z=4, sqrt(2)a=4r, CN=12, PE=74.0%).
HCP vs CCP: HCP is ABAB... packing (Z=6 per hexagonal prism, CN=12, PE=74.0%, volume = 24 sqrt(2) r^3); CCP/FCC is ABCABC... (Z=4, CN=12, PE=74.0%). Diamond cubic (Z=8, CN=4, PE=34%, sqrt(3)a = 8r).
2D Layer Packing: Square close packing (CN=4, PE=78.5%) vs Hexagonal close packing (CN=6, PE=90.7%).
Bragg's X-ray Diffraction Law: n * lambda = 2 * d_hkl * sin(theta), where interplanar spacing in cubic crystal d_hkl = a / sqrt(h^2 + k^2 + l^2).

sections.heading: Interstitial Voids, Ionic Crystal Lattices & Point Defects
sections.summary: Close-packed lattices of N spheres generate exactly N octahedral voids (6-coordinated, r/R = 0.414) and 2N tetrahedral voids (4-coordinated, r/R = 0.225). Ionic crystals adopt specific lattice prototypes based on cation-to-anion radius ratio, while point defects create non-stoichiometry, colour centres, and semiconduction.
keyPoints: Void Locations in FCC (Z = 4): 4 Octahedral voids (1 at body centre + 12 at edge centres x 1/4 = 4); 8 Tetrahedral voids (2 on each of 4 body diagonals at distance sqrt(3)a / 4 from corners; nearest tet-to-tet distance = a/2!).
Limiting Radius Ratio (r_+/r_-): <0.155 Linear (CN=2); 0.155-0.225 Trigonal planar (CN=3); 0.225-0.414 Tetrahedral (CN=4, ZnS); 0.414-0.732 Octahedral (CN=6, NaCl); 0.732-1.0 Cubic (CN=8, CsCl).

Ionic Prototypes: NaCl Rock Salt (Cl^- FCC, Na^+ all Oct voids -> 6:6, Z=4); CsCl (Cl^- SC, Cs^+ body centre -> 8:8, Z=1, heating to 760 K turns into NaCl!); ZnS Zinc Blende (S^2- FCC, Zn^2+ half Tet voids -> 4:4, Z=4); CaF2 Fluorite (Ca^2+ FCC, F^- ALL Tet voids -> 8:4, Z=4); Na2O Antifluorite (O^2- FCC, Na^+ ALL Tet voids -> 4:8, Z=4). Spinel AB2O4: normal puts A^2+ in 1/8 Tet & B^3+ in 1/2 Oct.

Stoichiometric Defects: Schottky (equal cation & anion vacancies -> DENSITY DROPS, high CN & similar ion sizes: NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr); Frenkel (small cation slips to interstitial void -> DENSITY UNCHANGED, low CN & large size gap: ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI). AgBr exhibits BOTH!

Non-Stoichiometric & Impurity Defects: Metal excess F-centres (heating NaCl in Na vapour -> trapped electrons give YELLOW colour & paramagnetism; LiCl pink, KCl violet!); Metal deficiency (Fe_0.93O -> some Fe^2+ replaced by fewer Fe^3+ p-type semiconductor); Doping Si/Ge with Group 15 (P, As -> n-type) vs Group 13 (B, Al, Ga -> p-type).

Distance between two nearest octahedral voids in FCC is a/sqrt(2), whereas distance between two nearest tetrahedral voids along a cell edge is a/2!
Diamond has a tetrahedral network with FCC lattice points + 4 atoms inside (Z = 8 total, packing efficiency ONLY 34% — NOT 74%!).

solvedExamples.question: Calculate the critical temperature T_c and critical pressure P_c of a van der Waals gas if its Boyle temperature T_B = 405 K and b = 0.04 L/mol (R = 0.0821 L.atm/mol.K).
steps: Recall exact universal ratio T_B / T_c = 27 / 8 => T_c = (8 / 27) * T_B = (8 / 27) * 405 = 120 K.
From T_B = a / (R b), solve for a: a = R * b * T_B = 0.0821 * 0.04 * 405 = 1.330 atm.L^2/mol^2.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using T_B = 2 T_c (that is Inversion Temp T_i = 2 T_B, NOT T_B = 2 T_c!).

solvedExamples.question: An element crystallizes in an FCC lattice with edge length a = 400 pm and density rho = 2.7 g/cm^3. Identify the atomic mass M of the element (N_A = 6.02 x 10^23).
steps: For FCC unit cell, Z = 4 atoms.
Convert edge length to cm: a = 400 pm = 4 x 10^(-8) cm => a^3 = 64 x 10^(-24) cm^3.
Use rho = (Z * M) / (N_A * a^3) => M = (rho * N_A * a^3) / Z.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Converting 1 pm = 10^(-12) cm instead of 10^(-10) cm (10^(-12) m) gives 10^6 density error!

solvedExamples.question: In a close-packed oxide lattice of O^2- ions, ferric ions (Fe^3+) occupy two-thirds of the octahedral voids while divalent M^2+ ions occupy one-eighth of the tetrahedral voids. Deduce the empirical formula.
steps: Let number of close-packed O^2- ions = N.
Number of octahedral voids = N => occupied by Fe^3+ = (2/3) N.
Number of tetrahedral voids = 2N => occupied by M^2+ = (1/8) * 2N = (1/4) N.

Ratio M : Fe : O = 1/4 : 2/3 : 1 (multiply by 12) = 3 : 8 : 12 => M3Fe8O12 (Check charge balance: 3(+2) + 8(+3) = +30 vs 12(-2) = -24 -> Wait: if 1/8 tet + 1/2 oct => 1:2:4 spinel! Here formula from counts is M3Fe8O12; for charge-neutral spinel 1/8 tet + 1/2 oct gives MFe2O4!).
solvedExamples.answer: Empirical ratio M3Fe8O12 from given fractions (note: charge-neutral spinel uses 1/8 tet + 1/2 oct = MFe2O4)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Taking tetrahedral voids = N instead of 2N halves the M^2+ count!

solvedExamples.question: A gas mixture of He and CH4 in a 4:1 molar ratio is allowed to effuse through a tiny pinhole into an evacuated vessel. Find the molar ratio of He to CH4 in the effused gas after two successive effusion stages (He = 4, CH4 = 16).
steps: After Stage 1: (n_He / n_CH4)_1 = (n_He / n_CH4)_0 * (P_He/P_CH4 cancels? No, rate ratio = (X_He / X_CH4) * sqrt(M_CH4 / M_He)).
Initial ratio = 4 / 1; sqrt(16 / 4) = sqrt(4) = 2.
So after Stage 1: (n_He / n_CH4)_1 = (4 / 1) * 2 = 8 : 1.
Collecting the effused gas and re-effusing through a second pinhole (Stage 2): (n_He / n_CH4)_2 = 8 * sqrt(16 / 4) = 8 * 2 = 16 : 1.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying sqrt(M1/M2) instead of sqrt(M2/M1) or forgetting that initial mole ratio multiplies into partial pressure ratio!

sections.heading: Adsorption Thermodynamics, Physisorption vs Chemisorption & Isotherms
sections.summary: Adsorption concentrates gas or solute molecules at a surface, lowering residual surface forces so Delta H < 0 while loss of translational freedom yields Delta S < 0. Consequently, adsorption proceeds spontaneously only at low temperatures where |Delta H| > |T Delta S| until equilibrium Delta G = 0.
keyPoints: Adsorption vs Absorption: Adsorption is strictly surface (silica gel + H2O vapour, charcoal + NH3); Absorption is bulk (anhydrous CaCl2 + H2O vapour); Sorption = both simultaneously (dyes on cotton).

Physisorption vs Chemisorption: Physisorption (weak van der Waals, non-specific, multilayer, Delta H ~ 20-40 kJ/mol, low Ea, decreases monotonically with T); Chemisorption (chemical bonds, highly specific, monolayer, Delta H ~ 80-240 kJ/mol, high Ea -> rises first then falls as T increases!).
Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm: x / m = k * P^(1/n) (n >= 1, so 0 <= 1/n <= 1). Linear log form: log(x/m) = log k + (1/n) log P (slope = 1/n, intercept = log k).

Pressure limits on Freundlich: Low P (1/n = 1 -> x/m proportional to P); Intermediate P (0 < 1/n < 1); Saturation High P (1/n -> 0 -> x/m = constant independent of P!). Note: Freundlich fails at very high pressure!
Langmuir Monolayer Isotherm (ideal uniform sites, no lateral interactions): theta = (K * P) / (1 + K * P), where K = k_ads / k_des.

sections.heading: Catalysis: Homogeneous, Heterogeneous, Zeolites & Enzymes
sections.summary: Catalysts open an alternate lower-activation-energy pathway without altering reaction thermodynamics (Delta H, Delta G, K_eq). Solid heterogeneous catalysts function via reactant adsorption, surface intermediate reaction, and product desorption, tuned by promoters and shape-selective micropores.
keyPoints: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous: Homogeneous (NO(g) in Lead Chamber SO2 oxidation, H^+ in ester hydrolysis); Heterogeneous (Fe/Mo in Haber NH3, Pt/Rh in Ostwald HNO3, V2O5 in Contact H2SO4, Ni in vegetable oil hydrogenation).
Promoters vs Poisons: Promoters (Mo for Fe in Haber) enhance catalyst activity; Poisons (As2O3, CO, Pb, Hg) block active sites irreversibly.
Activity vs Selectivity: CO + H2 gives CH4 over Ni, CH3OH over Cu/ZnO-Cr2O3, and HCHO over Cu!
Shape-Selective Catalysis (Zeolites): Honeycomb aluminosilicates with 260-740 pm pores; ZSM-5 converts alcohols directly into gasoline (petrol) by dehydrating inside size-selective cavities.
Enzyme Catalysis: Highly efficient (10^8-10^20x speedup), optimum T ~ 298-310 K, optimum pH ~ 5-7; Invertase, Zymase, Diastase, Maltase, Urease, Pepsin.

sections.heading: Colloidal Solutions: Classification, Micelles, Peptization & Purification
sections.summary: Colloids bridge true solutions and coarse suspensions with dispersed-phase particle sizes between 1 nm and 1000 nm, exhibiting heterogeneous optical scattering (Tyndall effect) and kinetic Brownian motion. Surfactants self-assemble into associated micelles strictly above both the Kraft Temperature (T_k) and Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC).
keyPoints: 8 Colloidal Types: Solid sol (alloys, ruby glass), Sol (paints, cell fluids, gold/As2S3), Aerosol of solid (smoke, dust), Gel (cheese, butter, jellies), Emulsion (milk, hair cream), Aerosol of liquid (fog, mist, clouds), Solid foam (pumice, rubber), Foam (froth, whipped cream). Gas-in-gas is ALWAYS homogeneous true solution!

Lyophilic (starch, gum, gelatin, egg albumin: reversible, self-stabilized, high viscosity, low surface tension) vs Lyophobic (Au, Ag, Fe(OH)3, As2S3: irreversible, require stabilizers, coagulate easily on adding small electrolyte!).

Structural classes: Multimolecular (S8 sol, Au sol); Macromolecular (starch, cellulose, proteins, nylon); Associated Micelles (soaps RCOONa above CMC ~ 10^(-4) - 10^(-3) M and Kraft temp T_k; hydrophilic head outside, hydrophobic tail inside!).

Preparation: Chemical double decomposition (As2O3 + 3 H2S -> As2S3 sol), Reduction (AuCl3 + HCHO -> Purple of Cassius Au sol), Oxidation (SO2 + 2 H2S -> S sol), Bredig's Arc (electrical dispersion + condensation for Au/Ag/Pt), Peptization (fresh ppt + common-ion electrolyte: Fe(OH)3 + FeCl3 -> positive Fe(OH)3 sol!).

Purification & Kinetics: Dialysis / Electrodialysis (removes crystalloid ions through parchment/cellophane), Ultrafiltration. Tyndall effect demands particle diameter >= wavelength & large refractive index difference (strong in lyophobic, weak in lyophilic); Brownian motion prevents gravity settling.

sections.heading: Electrical Double Layer, Hardy-Schulze Coagulation, Gold Number & Emulsions
sections.summary: Colloidal particles acquire uniform surface charge via preferential adsorption of common lattice ions, creating a fixed Stern layer and mobile diffuse layer whose potential difference (Zeta potential) prevents aggregation. Neutralizing this charge by oppositely charged ions triggers coagulation governed by Hardy-Schulze's fourth-power rule.
keyPoints: Charge Signs of Common Sols: POSITIVE sols = hydrated metal oxides (Fe2O3.xH2O, Cr2O3.xH2O, Al2O3.xH2O, TiO2), basic dyes (methylene blue), Haemoglobin! NEGATIVE sols = metals (Cu, Ag, Au), metal sulphides (As2S3, Sb2S3, CdS), acidic dyes (eosin, congo red), starch, gum, gelatin, clay, blood!
Preferential Ion Adsorption: AgNO3 + excess KI -> negatively charged AgI/I^- sol; KI + excess AgNO3 -> positively charged AgI/Ag^+ sol!

Electrophoresis & Electro-osmosis: Under electric field, charged dispersed particles migrate (electrophoresis); when colloid particles are immobilized by membrane, dispersion medium moves instead (electro-osmosis).

Hardy-Schulze Rule: Coagulation power increases drastically with valency of oppositely charged flocculating ion (proportional to z^4 - z^6)! For negative As2S3 sol: Al^3+ > Ba^2+ > Na^+; for positive Fe(OH)3 sol: [Fe(CN)6]^4- > PO4^3- > SO4^2- > Cl^-. (Flocculation value = millimoles/L needed -> INVERSE of coagulating power!).

Gold Number (Zsigmondy): Minimum mg of protective lyophilic colloid preventing coagulation of 10 mL standard red gold sol by 1 mL of 10% NaCl! LOWER Gold Number = HIGHER protective power: Gelatin (0.005) > Haemoglobin (0.03) > Egg Albumin (0.1) > Gum Arabic (0.15) > Potato Starch (25).

Emulsions: Oil-in-Water (O/W: milk, vanishing cream -> water-soluble dye spreads, high conductivity) vs Water-in-Oil (W/O: butter, cold cream, cod liver oil -> oil-soluble dye spreads, low conductivity). Bancroft's rule: continuous phase is the one in which emulsifier dissolves better!

sections.heading: Advanced Electrochemistry: Concentration Cells, Reference Electrodes & Cell dE/dT
sections.summary: Concentration cells generate EMF solely from activity gradients between identical electrodes (E deg_cell = 0 identically), driving spontaneous equalization until C_cathode = C_anode. Measuring cell EMF temperature coefficient (dE/dT)_P directly yields exact reaction entropy Delta S and enthalpy Delta H via Gibbs-Helmholtz.
keyPoints: Electrolyte Concentration Cell (without transference): M | M^(n+)(C1) || M^(n+)(C2) | M has E_cell = (0.0591 / n) log10(C2 / C1) at 298 K; spontaneous ONLY when C2 (cathode) > C1 (anode)! Anion cell Pt(Cl2) | Cl^-(C1) || Cl^-(C2) | Pt(Cl2) needs C1 (anode) > C2 (cathode)!

Electrode Concentration Cell (amalgam / gas): Pt(H2, P1) | H^+ | Pt(H2, P2) has E_cell = (0.0591 / 2) log10(P1 / P2) (spontaneous when P1 > P2!); Zn-Hg(C1) | Zn^2+ | Zn-Hg(C2) has E_cell = (0.0591 / 2) log10(C1 / C2).
Calomel Reference Electrode: Hg(l) | Hg2Cl2(s) | KCl(aq); half-cell Hg2Cl2 + 2e^- <-> 2 Hg + 2 Cl^-; saturated KCl gives E_SRP = +0.242 V (constant independent of external solution!).
Silver-Silver Chloride & Ksp Cell: Ag | AgCl(s) | Cl^-(aq) has E deg(Cl^-/AgCl/Ag) = E deg(Ag^+/Ag) + 0.0591 * log10(K_sp(AgCl))!
Quinhydrone pH Electrode: Pt | Q, H2Q, H^+(pH) -> Q + 2H^+ + 2e^- <=> H2Q; E = E deg - 0.0591 * pH (fails above pH 8 due to hydroquinone ionization).
Gibbs-Helmholtz Cell Thermodynamics: Delta G = -n F E; Delta S = -(dDeltaG/dT)_P = n F (dE/dT)_P; Delta H = Delta G + T Delta S = -n F [E - T(dE/dT)_P]!

derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Enables exact extraction of Delta G, Delta S, and Delta H from two EMF measurements at T1 and T2.

solvedExamples.question: Calculate the minimum mass of Gelatin (Gold Number = 0.005) and Potato Starch (Gold Number = 25) required to prevent coagulation of 100 mL of standard gold sol upon adding 10 mL of 10% NaCl solution.
steps: Recall definition of Gold Number: mass in milligrams (mg) required for 10 mL of gold sol + 1 mL of 10% NaCl.
Here both gold sol volume (100 mL = 10 x 10 mL) and 10% NaCl volume (10 mL = 10 x 1 mL) are scaled 10-fold.
Minimum Gelatin needed = 10 x 0.005 mg = 0.05 mg.
Minimum Potato Starch needed = 10 x 25 mg = 250 mg (0.25 g).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying Gold Number directly without scaling 10 mL -> 100 mL (factor of 10)!

solvedExamples.question: In a Freundlich adsorption experiment, a plot of log(x/m) vs log P gives a straight line with slope 0.5 and y-intercept log(2). Calculate x/m at P = 9 atm.
steps: Freundlich linear equation: log10(x/m) = log10(k) + (1/n) log10(P).
Compare with line: slope 1/n = 0.5 = 1/2, intercept log10(k) = log10(2) => k = 2.
Substitute into x/m = k * P^(1/n) = 2 * (9)^(0.5).
x/m = 2 * 3 = 6 (g gas adsorbed per g adsorbent).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Taking k = log(2) = 0.301 instead of reading y-intercept as log(k) => k = 2!

solvedExamples.question: 100 mL of 0.01 M AgNO3 is mixed with 100 mL of 0.02 M KI to prepare a colloidal AgI sol. Determine the surface charge on the sol and arrange NaCl, BaCl2, and AlCl3 in decreasing order of coagulating power for this sol.
steps: Compute millimoles: AgNO3 = 100 x 0.01 = 1 mmol; KI = 100 x 0.02 = 2 mmol.
Ag^+ + I^- -> AgI(sol) + 1 mmol excess I^- remaining in solution.
AgI preferentially adsorbs the common excess lattice ion I^- -> forms NEGATIVELY charged AgI/I^- sol!
By Hardy-Schulze rule, coagulation of a negative sol requires CATIONS of highest valency: Al^3+ (AlCl3) > Ba^2+ (BaCl2) > Na^+ (NaCl).
solvedExamples.answer: Negative AgI/I^- sol; coagulating power AlCl3 > BaCl2 > NaCl
solvedExamples.pitfall: Thinking Cl^- coagulates the negative sol instead of the oppositely charged cations!

solvedExamples.question: For the cell Ag(s) | AgCl(s) | KCl(0.1 M) || AgNO3(0.1 M) | Ag(s) at 298 K, given K_sp(AgCl) = 1.0 x 10^(-10), calculate the cell EMF and verify spontaneity direction.
steps: At cathode (right): [Ag^+]_R = 0.1 M = 10^(-1) M.
This reduces to an Ag^+ concentration cell (n = 1, E deg_cell = 0): E_cell = (0.0591 / 1) log10([Ag^+]_R / [Ag^+]_L).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using [Cl^-] = 0.1 M directly inside log ratio instead of converting it to [Ag^+]_L = K_sp / [Cl^-]!

sections.heading: Hydrogen, Isotopes, Water Hardness & Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2)
sections.summary: Hydrogen displays unique reactivity across ionic saline, covalent molecular, and non-stoichiometric metallic hydrides while ortho- and para-H2 differ in nuclear spin alignment. H2O2 adopts a non-planar open-book geometry and functions as both oxidant and reductant across acidic and alkaline media.
keyPoints: Isotopes: Protium (1H, no neutron), Deuterium (2H, heavy water D2O moderator/tracer), Tritium (3H, beta^- emitter, t_1/2 = 12.33 yr). Bond energy D2 > H2 -> D2 reacts slower (kinetic isotope effect!).

Hydrides: Ionic/Saline (NaH, CaH2 hydrolith -> H2 with water); Covalent/Molecular (electron-deficient B2H6, precise CH4, rich NH3/H2O/HF); Metallic/Interstitial (TiH_1.7, PdH_0.6 -> H2 storage; Groups 7,8,9 HYDRIDE GAP except CrH!).

Water Hardness: Temporary (Ca/Mg(HCO3)2 -> removed by boiling or Clark's Ca(OH)2); Permanent (Ca/Mg chlorides & sulphates -> removed by Washing soda Na2CO3, Calgon Na6P6O18 forming soluble [Na4P6O18]^2- complex, Permutit zeolite NaAlSiO4, or synthetic cation/anion ion-exchange resins for demineralized water!).
H2O2 Structure & Strength: Non-planar open-book (dihedral angle ~111.5 deg gas / ~90.2 deg solid; O-O = 147 pm). Volume strength V = 11.2 * M = 5.6 * N.

H2O2 Dual Redox: Oxidant (PbS black -> PbSO4 white, Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+, I^- -> I2, Cr(OH)3 -> CrO4^2- in base); Reductant (MnO4^- -> Mn^2+ + O2 in acid, MnO4^- -> MnO2 + O2 in base, Ag2O -> Ag + O2, O3 -> O2).

sections.heading: s-Block Group 1 (Alkali Metals): Liquid NH3, Oxides & Solvay Process
sections.summary: Alkali metals have large atomic radii and lowest first ionization enthalpies in their periods, acting as fierce reductants (Li strongest in water due to tiny Li^+ hydration energy despite highest IE1). Solutions in liquid ammonia liberate ammoniated electrons yielding paramagnetic deep-blue conductors.
keyPoints: Liquid NH3 Solutions: M + (x+y)NH3 -> [M(NH3)_x]^+ + [e(NH3)_y]^- (dilute = deep blue, paramagnetic, conducting!). Above ~3 M turns BRONZE-coloured and DIAMAGNETIC due to electron-pair spin coupling! Traces of Fe^3+ catalyze slow decomposition to MNH2 + 1/2 H2.
Oxides with excess O2: Li -> Li2O (normal oxide); Na -> Na2O2 (peroxide, diamagnetic); K, Rb, Cs -> MO2 (KO2 superoxide, paramagnetic 1 unpaired e-, releases O2 + CO2 scrubbing in submarines!).

Diagonal Li-Mg similarity: LiCl & MgCl2 are deliquescent & soluble in ethanol; LiNO3 & Mg(NO3)2 decompose on heating to Oxide + NO2 + O2 (whereas Na/K/Rb/Cs nitrates give Nitrite MNO2 + O2 ONLY!); Li2CO3 decomposes to Li2O + CO2 (other M2CO3 thermally stable!); ONLY Li forms Li3N directly with N2.

Alkali Halide melting & solubility: MF MP drops down group (lattice energy), while LiF is sparingly soluble in water (high lattice) and CsI is sparingly soluble (low hydration); LiI is soluble in organic solvents (Fajan's rule!).

Solvay Ammonia-Soda Process (Na2CO3): NH3 + H2O + CO2 + NaCl -> NaHCO3(ppt) + NH4Cl; 2 NaHCO3 -(heat)-> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; NH3 recovered via Ca(OH)2 (CaCl2 byproduct!). FAILS for K2CO3 because KHCO3 is too soluble in water to precipitate!

sections.heading: s-Block Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals): Anomalies, Plaster of Paris & Cement
sections.summary: Group 2 metals exhibit +2 oxidation state with smaller radii and higher ionization enthalpies than Group 1. Beryllium shows stark covalent diagonal similarity to Aluminium, while hydration-vs-lattice enthalpy competition reverses solubility trends between Group 2 hydroxides and sulphates.
keyPoints: Diagonal Be-Al similarity: Both form protective oxide films resisting conc HNO3; Be(OH)2 & Al(OH)3 are AMPHOTERIC ([Be(OH)4]^2- & [Al(OH)4]^-); BeCl2 (polymeric chain in solid, bridged dimer in vapour) and AlCl3 act as covalent Friedel-Crafts Lewis acids; Be2C & Al4C3 yield METHANE (CH4) on hydrolysis (whereas CaC2 gives ethyne C2H2 & Mg2C3 gives propyne!).

Solubility Opposites: Hydroxides & Fluorides INCREASE down group (Be(OH)2 < Mg(OH)2 < Ca(OH)2 < Sr(OH)2 < Ba(OH)2); Sulphates, Carbonates & Chromates DECREASE down group (BeSO4 > MgSO4 > CaSO4 > SrSO4 > BaSO4 insoluble!).
Thermal Stability: MCO3, M(OH)2, MSO4, M(NO3)2 thermal decomposition temperature INCREASES down the group (BeCO3 unstable, kept in CO2!).

Plaster of Paris & Gypsum: CaSO4.2H2O (Gypsum) at 393 K (120 C) -> CaSO4.1/2 H2O (Plaster of Paris, sets exothermically with water back to gypsum!). Above 473 K gives anhydrous CaSO4 (dead burnt plaster — fails to set!).
Portland Cement: CaO (50-60%), SiO2 (20-25%), Al2O3 (5-10%), MgO (2-3%), Fe2O3 (1-2%), SO3. Setting = hydration + gel formation; Gypsum (2-3%) is added to SLOW DOWN setting time!

sections.heading: Boron & Silicon Chemistry: Diborane, Borax, Boric Acid, Silicates & Silicones
sections.summary: Boron forms electron-deficient 3c-2e banana-bonded hydrides and planar hexagonal B3N3H6 borazine, while orthoboric acid acts as a weak monobasic OH^- acceptor stabilized by cis-diols. Silicon builds rigid 3D silicates from corner-shared SiO4^4- tetrahedra and flexible water-repellent silicone polymers.
keyPoints: Borax (Na2B4O7.10H2O = Na2[B4O5(OH)4].8H2O): Contains TWO sp3 tetrahedral B and TWO sp2 trigonal planar B! Aqueous solution is alkaline (1 mol Borax consumes 2 mol HCl -> 4 H3BO3). Heating swells into glassy NaBO2 + B2O3 bead (Cu^2+ blue, Co^2+ deep blue, Fe^3+ yellow, Cr^3+ green).

Orthoboric Acid (H3BO3): Layered 2D H-bonded sheets (slippery). Weak MONOBASIC Lewis acid: H3BO3 + 2 H2O <=> [B(OH)4]^- + H3O^+ (cannot be titrated directly with NaOH UNLESS cis-diol like glycerol/mannitol is added to chelate [B(OH)4]^-!).

Diborane (B2H6): 4 terminal 2c-2e B-H bonds (coplanar with 2 B = 6 coplanar atoms!) + 2 bridging 3c-2e B-H-B banana bonds (perpendicular!). Prep: BF3 + LiAlH4 or NaBH4 + I2. Symmetric cleavage (with NMe3/CO -> 2 BH3.L) vs Unsymmetric cleavage (with NH3/EtNH2 -> [BH2(NH3)2]^+[BH4]^-; heating at 473 K gives Borazine B3N3H6 'inorganic benzene'!).

Silicates (SiO4^4- corner-shared O count s): s=0 Orthosilicate (SiO4^4-, zircon); s=1 Pyrosilicate (Si2O7^6-, thortveitite); s=2 Cyclic/Chain (SiO3^2-, beryl Be3Al2Si6O18, pyroxenes); s=2.5 Double chain amphibole (Si4O11^6-, asbestos); s=3 Sheet (Si2O5^2-, talc, mica, clay); s=4 3D Framework (SiO2 quartz, feldspar, zeolites when Al^3+ replaces Si^4+!).
Silicones (R2SiO)_n: Hydrolysis of R2SiCl2 yields linear polymer (RSiCl3 -> cross-linked resin; R3SiCl -> chain-terminating blocker!). Water-repellent, thermally stable electrical insulators.

sections.heading: Metallurgy I: Ore Concentration, Roasting & Ellingham Diagrams
sections.summary: Extracting metals from ores follows concentration (froth flotation for sulphides, magnetic separation, leaching), conversion to oxides (calcination or roasting), and thermodynamic reduction governed by Ellingham plots (Delta G deg vs T). Lower lines on the Ellingham diagram spontaneously reduce metal oxides sitting above them.
keyPoints: Major Ores: Oxide (Haematite Fe2O3, Magnetite Fe3O4, Bauxite Al2O3.xH2O, Cassiterite SnO2, Cuprite Cu2O, Pyrolusite MnO2); Sulphide (Copper pyrites CuFeS2, Galena PbS, Zinc blende ZnS, Cinnabar HgS, Argentite Ag2S); Carbonate (Siderite FeCO3, Calamine ZnCO3, Malachite CuCO3.Cu(OH)2, Dolomite); Halide (Cryolite Na3AlF6, Horn silver AgCl, Carnallite).
Froth Flotation (Sulphide ores): Pine oil/eucalyptus (frother) + Ethyl xanthate (collector) + NaCN (depressant prevents ZnS from floating so PbS separates cleanly from ZnS!).
Calcination (heating carbonate/hydrated oxide in ABSENCE/limited air -> CO2/H2O loss) vs Roasting (heating sulphide in EXCESS air -> oxide + SO2).

Ellingham Diagram Slopes (2xM + O2 -> 2 M_xO, Delta G deg vs T): Most metal oxidation lines slope UPWARD (Delta S < 0, O2 gas consumed); sharp upward kinks occur at metal boiling points (e.g. Mg boils 1366 K -> steep jump!).

Carbon lines on Ellingham: C + O2 -> CO2 has ~ZERO slope (Delta n_g = 0); 2 C + O2 -> 2 CO slopes DOWNWARD (Delta S > 0!) cutting across metal oxide lines at high T; 2 CO + O2 -> 2 CO2 slopes UPWARD! Below 983 K (710 C), CO reduces Fe2O3; above 983 K, Coke C reduces FeO directly (Mg reduces Al2O3 below ~1623 K; above 1623 K Al can reduce MgO!).

sections.heading: Metallurgy II: Extraction of Fe, Cu, Al, Ag/Au & Refining Techniques
sections.summary: Reactive electropositive metals (Al, Na, Mg) require electrolytic reduction whereas moderate metals (Fe, Zn, Pb, Cu) undergo pyrometallurgical smelting or auto-reduction. Ultrapure metals for catalysis and semiconductors rely on chemical vapour transport (Mond, van Arkel) and Zone Refining.
keyPoints: Iron (Blast Furnace): Haematite + Coke + Limestone CaCO3 (flux removes SiO2 gangue as fusible CaSiO3 slag!). 500-800 K: Fe2O3 -> Fe3O4 -> FeO by CO; 900-1500 K: FeO + C -> Fe + CO. Pig iron (4% C) -> Cast iron (3% C) -> Wrought iron (<0.5% C, purest commercial!).
Copper (CuFeS2): Roasted + SiO2 -> FeSiO3 slag removed, leaving Copper matte (Cu2S + FeS). Bessemer converter auto-reduction: 2 Cu2O + Cu2S -> 6 Cu + SO2 (escaping SO2 gives Blister Copper!).

Aluminium: Baeyer's leaching (red bauxite with Fe2O3 impurity -> NaOH dissolves Al2O3 as [Al(OH)4]^-, Fe2O3 insoluble; white bauxite with SiO2 uses Serpeck's N2/C); Hall-Heroult electrolysis of Al2O3 dissolved in molten Cryolite (Na3AlF6) + Fluorspar (CaF2) lowers MP (~1140 K) & raises conductivity (graphite anodes burn to CO/CO2!).
Silver & Gold (MacArthur-Forrest Cyanide Leaching): 4 Au + 8 CN^- + 2 H2O + O2 -> 4 [Au(CN)2]^- + 4 OH^-; displaced by Zn dust: 2 [Au(CN)2]^- + Zn -> [Zn(CN)4]^2- + 2 Au!

Metal Refining: Liquation (low MP Sn, Pb, Bi); Distillation (volatile Zn, Cd, Hg); Poling (green wood logs reduce Cu2O in blister Cu); Cupellation (Pb impurity oxidized from Ag/Au); Electrolytic (Cu, Ag, Au, Zn, Al Hoope's); Mond's Process (Ni + 4 CO at 330-350 K -> Ni(CO)4 -> 450-470 K pure Ni!); Van Arkel-de Boer (Zr/Ti + 2 I2 at 870 K -> ZrI4 -> W filament 2075 K pure Zr/Ti!); Zone Refining (Si, Ge, Ga, B, In — impurities more soluble in melt!).

solvedExamples.question: Calculate the volume strength and % (w/v) of a 2.0 M H2O2 solution, and find the volume of O2 liberated at STP (22.4 L/mol) by decomposing 100 mL of this solution.
steps: Volume strength V = 11.2 * Molarity = 11.2 * 2.0 = 22.4 V.
Mass per litre = Molarity * Molar mass = 2.0 * 34 = 68 g/L => in 100 mL = 6.8 g => % (w/v) = 6.8%.
By definition of 22.4 V, 1 L of this H2O2 liberates 22.4 L O2 at STP (22.4 L/mol).
Therefore, 100 mL (0.1 L) liberates 0.1 * 22.4 = 2.24 L of O2.
solvedExamples.answer: Volume strength = 22.4 V, 6.8% (w/v), 2.24 L O2 liberated
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using n-factor = 1 instead of 2 (gives 11.2 instead of 5.6 for Normality, or halving/doubling M).

solvedExamples.question: Determine the anionic repeat-unit formula of (a) Pyrosilicate, (b) Single-chain Pyroxene, (c) Sheet silicate, and count how many oxygen atoms each SiO4 tetrahedron shares in each.
steps: General rule: each shared corner reduces oxygen count per Si by 0.5 and negative charge by 1: SiO_(4 - s/2)^(-(4 - s)).
(a) Pyrosilicate shares s = 1 corner between two tetrahedra: 2 x [SiO_3.5]^(-3) = Si2O7^6-.
(b) Single-chain Pyroxene shares s = 2 corners per tetrahedron: SiO_(4 - 1)^(-(4 - 2)) = (SiO3^2-)_n.
(c) Sheet silicate shares s = 3 corners: [SiO_2.5]^(-1) = (Si2O5^2-)_n.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing double-chain amphibole (Si4O11^6-, alternating 2 and 3 shared) with sheet silicate (Si2O5^2-, all 3 shared)!

solvedExamples.question: Explain why (i) KO2 is paramagnetic and coloured, (ii) LiF is nearly insoluble in water whereas LiCl dissolves in acetone, and (iii) Boric acid behaves as a weak monobasic acid.
steps: (i) KO2 contains superoxide ion O2^- (17 e-, MOT config ends in pi*2p^3), which has 1 unpaired electron -> paramagnetic and yellow-orange!
(ii) Li^+ and F^- are both tiny -> lattice enthalpy of LiF exceeds combined hydration enthalpies -> sparingly soluble in water.
In contrast, LiCl has strong covalent character (Fajan's rule: tiny Li^+ strongly polarizes Cl^-) -> dissolves in polar organic solvents like acetone!
(iii) H3BO3 has an incomplete boron octet (6 e-), so it accepts OH^- from water (B(OH)3 + 2 H2O -> [B(OH)4]^- + H3O^+) rather than releasing its own protons -> weak monobasic Lewis acid.
solvedExamples.answer: KO2 has 1 unpaired pi* e-; LiF high lattice enthalpy vs LiCl Fajan covalency; H3BO3 accepts 1 OH^-
solvedExamples.pitfall: Treating H3BO3 as a tribasic Bronsted acid because it has 3 hydrogens!

solvedExamples.question: On the Ellingham diagram, the line for 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO lies BELOW 4/3 Al + O2 -> 2/3 Al2O3 below 1623 K, and crosses ABOVE it above 1623 K. Predict which metal reduces the other's oxide at 1200 K vs 1800 K, and explain the sharp kink in Mg's line near 1366 K.
steps: At 1200 K (< 1623 K), Delta G deg(Mg -> MgO) < Delta G deg(Al -> Al2O3). Subtracting gives negative Delta G deg for 3 Mg + Al2O3 -> 3 MgO + 2 Al => Mg reduces Al2O3!
At 1366 K, Magnesium boils (liquid -> gas)! Formation of MgO now consumes BOTH Mg(g) and O2(g), making Delta S much more negative.
Because slope = -Delta S, the Mg/MgO line bends sharply UPWARD at 1366 K and soon crosses ABOVE the Al/Al2O3 line at 1623 K.
Consequently at 1800 K (> 1623 K), Al sits lower and can reduce MgO (3 MgO + 2 Al -> Al2O3 + 3 Mg(g) distilling off)!
solvedExamples.answer: 1200 K: Mg reduces Al2O3; 1366 K kink = Mg boiling (Delta S more negative); 1800 K: Al reduces MgO
solvedExamples.pitfall: Thinking Ellingham lines bend downward at metal boiling points — consuming gaseous metal makes Delta S MORE negative so slope bends UPWARD!

sections.heading: Polymerization Mechanisms, PDI & Commercial Addition Polymers
sections.summary: Addition (chain-growth) polymers build high-MW chains from unsaturated monomers via free-radical, cationic, anionic, or coordination Ziegler-Natta mechanisms without losing small molecules. Synthetic rubbers, Teflon, PVC, and PAN arise from stereoregular or copolymer chain additions.
keyPoints: Molecular Weight Distribution: Number-average M_n = Sum(N_i M_i)/Sum(N_i); Weight-average M_w = Sum(N_i M_i^2)/Sum(N_i M_i). Polydispersity Index PDI = M_w / M_n (always >= 1 for synthetic polymers; = 1 strictly for monodisperse natural proteins/enzymes!).

LDPE vs HDPE: LDPE (high P 1000-2000 atm, 350-570 K, O2/peroxide radical -> branched, low density, flexible); HDPE (low P 6-7 atm, 333-343 K, Ziegler-Natta TiCl4 + Al(C2H5)3 -> linear, high density, tough!).
Homopolymers: PTFE/Teflon (CF2=CF2, ammonium persulphate catalyst, inert non-stick); PAN/Orlon/Acrilan (CH2=CH-CN); PVC (CH2=CH-Cl); Polystyrene (Ph-CH=CH2); PMMA (methyl methacrylate -> Plexiglas!).

Natural vs Vulcanized Rubber: Natural rubber = ALL-CIS 1,4-polyisoprene (from 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene); Gutta-percha = ALL-TRANS 1,4-polyisoprene (hard, non-elastic!). Vulcanization heats natural rubber with 3-5% Sulphur -> forms S-S disulphide crosslinks (30% S gives rigid Ebonite!).

Synthetic Rubbers: Neoprene (polychloroprene from CH2=C(Cl)-CH=CH2 -> oil-resistant); Buna-S (1,3-butadiene + styrene, Na radical -> tyres); Buna-N (1,3-butadiene + acrylonitrile -> oil seals, resistant to petrol!).

sections.heading: Condensation, Cross-Linked & Biodegradable Polymers
sections.summary: Step-growth condensation polymers eliminate H2O, CH3OH, or NH3 between bifunctional or polyfunctional monomers to construct polyamides, polyesters, and 3D thermoset resins. Biodegradable aliphatic polyesters and polyamides break down cleanly under environmental hydrolysis.
keyPoints: Polyamides: Nylon-6,6 (Hexamethylenediamine + Adipic acid, 553 K); Nylon-6 (Caprolactam ring-opening hydrolysis at 533-543 K -> single 6-C monomer!); Nylon-6,10 (Hexamethylenediamine + Sebacic acid).
Polyesters: Terylene / Dacron (Ethylene glycol + Terephthalic acid, Zn(OAc)2-Sb2O3 catalyst at 420-460 K -> crease-resistant fibre); Glyptal (Ethylene glycol + Phthalic acid -> paints/lacquers).

Thermosetting Resins: Bakelite (Phenol + Formaldehyde -> initial acid/base condensation gives linear Novolac; heating Novolac with excess HCHO yields cross-linked 3D Bakelite!); Melamine-formaldehyde (Melamine + HCHO -> unbreakable crockery); Urea-formaldehyde.
Thermoplastics (linear/lightly branched, soften repeatedly on heating: Polythene, Polystyrene, PVC) vs Thermosets (heavily cross-linked, infusible once set: Bakelite, Melamine resin).

Biodegradable Polymers: PHBV (Poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate-co-beta-hydroxyvalerate from 3-hydroxybutanoic acid + 3-hydroxypentanoic acid -> orthopaedic packaging/drug release); Nylon-2-nylon-6 (Glycine + 6-aminocaproic acid!).

sections.heading: Advanced Named Rearrangements & C-C Bond Cascades
sections.summary: JEE Advanced multi-step problems weave classical carbocation, nitrene, carbanion, and pericyclic rearrangements into stereospecific synthesis chains. Tracking migratory aptitude and orbital geometry prevents regiochemical traps.
keyPoints: Beckmann Rearrangement: Ketoxime + H2SO4/PCl5/SOCl2 -> substituted amide; ALWAYS migrates the group ANTI (trans) to the leaving -OH! (Hydrolyze amide -> identifies original ketone stereochemistry!).
Favorskii & Benzilic Acid Rearrangements: Alpha-halo ketone + alkoxide -> ring-contracted ester via cyclopropanone; Benzil (Ph-CO-CO-Ph) + KOH -> Benzilic acid (Ph2C(OH)COOH).

Claisen & Fries Rearrangements: Allyl aryl ether -(200 C)-> o-allylphenol ([3,3]-sigmatropic shift with allylic inversion; goes para if both ortho blocked!); Phenyl ester + AlCl3 -> o/p-acylphenol (Fries: low T favors para, high T favors ortho!).
Michael Addition + Robinson Annulation: Enolate (1,4-conjugate addition to alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone) followed by intramolecular aldol condensation builds fused 6-membered cyclohexenone rings!
Diels-Alder [4+2] Cycloaddition: Conjugated s-cis diene + electron-poor dienophile -> cyclohexene; stereospecific SYN addition (cis-dienophile -> cis-substituents) with ENDO kinetic preference!

sections.heading: Multi-Step Organic Roadmaps & Protecting-Group Strategy
sections.summary: Multi-step roadmaps chain functional conversions through chemoselective reagents and reversible protecting groups so incompatible functional groups survive harsh intermediates. Counting DBE and tracking stereocentres at every step isolates unique structural solutions.
keyPoints: Protecting Groups: Ketone/Aldehyde protected as cyclic acetal/ketal (ethylene glycol / H^+ -> completely stable to Grignard, LiAlH4, NaOH, then deprotected by H3O^+!); 1 deg/2 deg Alcohol protected as THP or TBDMS; Amine protected as acetamide (-NHCOCH3).

Selective Oxidations: SeO2 (Riley oxidation) converts allylic/alpha-CH2 next to C=O into C=O or allylic -OH; HIO4 (periodic acid) / Pb(OAc)4 cleaves vicinal diols, alpha-hydroxy ketones & alpha-diketones cleanly (1 mol HIO4 per C-C bond cleaved!).
Wolff-Kishner vs Raney-Ni Mozingo: Use thioacetal (HSCH2CH2SH/BF3) + Raney Ni to reduce C=O -> CH2 at NEUTRAL pH when BOTH acid-sensitive and base-sensitive groups exist!
Ozone + Aldol + Haloform Cascades: Common JEE Adv pattern -> Ozonolysis -> Intramolecular Aldol -> NaBH4 -> H2SO4/heat -> Br2/NaOH!

Chemoselective Hydride & Coupling Ladder: NaBH3CN reduces iminium ions selectively at pH 4-6 (reductive amination); DIBAL-H at -78 C stops esters/nitriles at aldehydes; Gilman R2CuLi couples cleanly with R'-X/R'COCl without adding to ketones/esters!

sections.heading: Quantitative Organic Analysis: Liebig, Dumas, Kjeldahl & Carius
sections.summary: Elemental mass percentages establish empirical formulas from combustion CO2/H2O (Liebig), volumetric N2 (Dumas), acid-back-titrated NH3 (Kjeldahl), and precipitated silver halide or barium sulphate (Carius). Molecular mass methods (Victor Meyer, silver salt, chloroplatinate) yield the exact molecular formula.
keyPoints: Liebig C & H Estimation: %C = (12/44) * (m_CO2 / w) * 100; %H = (2/18) * (m_H2O / w) * 100 (CO2 absorbed in KOH U-tube, H2O absorbed in anhydrous CaCl2!).

Dumas Nitrogen (Universal for ALL N compounds!): Organic N heated with CuO -> N2(g) collected over KOH (absorbs CO2); %N = (28 * V_N2(STP mL) / 22400) * (100 / w). Always subtract aqueous tension from total pressure before converting V_N2 to STP!

Kjeldahl Nitrogen: Heat with conc H2SO4 (+ CuSO4/K2SO4) -> (NH4)2SO4 + NaOH -> NH3 absorbed in excess H2SO4 -> back-titrate with NaOH! %N = (1.4 * N_acid_used * V_acid(mL)) / w(g). FAILS for -NO2, azo (-N=N-), diazonium, and ring N (pyridine, pyrrole)!

Carius Halogen, Sulphur & Phosphorus: Heat with fuming HNO3 (+ AgNO3 for X): %X = (AtWt(X) / MolWt(AgX)) * (m_AgX / w) * 100. For S (+ BaCl2 -> BaSO4): %S = (32 / 233) * (m_BaSO4 / w) * 100. For P: %P = (62 / 222) * (m_Mg2P2O7 / w) * 100 or (31 / 1877) * (m_phosphomolybdate / w) * 100.

Equivalent & Molecular Weights: Silver salt of n-basic acid (R(COOAg)_n -> n Ag on ignition): Eq.Wt(Acid) = (108 * w_salt / w_Ag) - 107! Chloroplatinate of monoacidic base (B2H2PtCl6 -> Pt): Eq.Wt(Base) = [(w_salt / w_Pt) * 195 - 410] / 2.

solvedExamples.question: A synthetic polymer sample contains 100 molecules of molar mass 10,000 g/mol and 200 molecules of molar mass 25,000 g/mol. Calculate M_n, M_w, and Polydispersity Index (PDI).
steps: PDI = M_w / M_n = 22,500 / 20,000 = 1.125 (> 1, confirming synthetic polydispersity).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Computing PDI = M_n / M_w (< 1) instead of M_w / M_n (> 1)!

solvedExamples.question: In Kjeldahl's estimation, ammonia evolved from 0.50 g of an organic compound was passed into 50 mL of 0.25 M H2SO4. The excess acid required 30 mL of 0.5 M NaOH for complete neutralization. Find % of Nitrogen.
steps: Initial mEq of H2SO4 = (0.25 M * 2) N * 50 mL = 0.50 N * 50 = 25 mEq.
Excess H2SO4 neutralized by NaOH = 0.5 M * 1 * 30 mL = 15 mEq.
Net mEq of H2SO4 consumed by NH3 = 25 - 15 = 10 mEq.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting to multiply 0.25 M H2SO4 by 2 to get Normality = 0.50 N!

solvedExamples.question: Identify the monomers and polymer class for (i) PHBV, (ii) Nylon-6, (iii) Buna-N, and (iv) Bakelite.
steps: (i) PHBV: 3-hydroxybutanoic acid + 3-hydroxypentanoic acid -> Biodegradable aliphatic polyester.
(ii) Nylon-6: Caprolactam (6-membered cyclic amide lactam) -> Condensation polyamide.
(iii) Buna-N: 1,3-butadiene + Acrylonitrile (CH2=CH-CN) -> Addition copolymer elastomer.
(iv) Bakelite: Phenol + Formaldehyde -> Cross-linked thermosetting condensation polymer.
solvedExamples.answer: PHBV (biodegradable polyester); Nylon-6 (polyamide); Buna-N (copolymer elastomer); Bakelite (thermoset)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing Buna-N (acrylonitrile) with Buna-S (styrene) or Nylon-6 (caprolactam) with Nylon-6,6!

solvedExamples.question: Compound A (C8H8O) reacts with NH2OH to give predominantly oxime B (with -OH anti to phenyl ring). Treating B with PCl5 yields amide C, which upon hydrolysis gives D + E. D gives a positive Carbylamine test and E gives brisk CO2 effervescence with NaHCO3. Identify A, B, C, D, E and verify the role of Beckmann stereochemistry.
steps: DBE of A (C8H8O) = 8 + 1 - 8/2 = 5 (benzene ring = 4 + one C=O = 1) => Acetophenone (Ph-CO-CH3)!
With NH2OH, A forms acetophenone oxime B: (E)-Ph-C(CH3)=N-OH (bulky Ph sits anti to -OH, while CH3 sits syn to -OH).
Beckmann rearrangement (PCl5) migrates the group ANTI to -OH (Phenyl!) onto Nitrogen => C is Acetanilide (Ph-NH-CO-CH3)!
Acid hydrolysis of C gives D = Aniline (Ph-NH2, positive Carbylamine 1 deg amine!) and E = Acetic acid (CH3COOH, CO2 with NaHCO3).
solvedExamples.answer: A = Acetophenone, B = (E)-Acetophenone oxime, C = Acetanilide, D = Aniline, E = Acetic acid
solvedExamples.pitfall: Migrating -CH3 instead of anti-Phenyl gives N-methylbenzamide -> Methylamine + Benzoic acid (wrong products)!
